reason: The mill, rowing club and allotments are places where people gather and support one another; losing them breaks the bonds of a community. The eels, willows and herons endure under both plans' complement, but I weigh human ties first.
Plan 2 saves the reed-cutting trade, a living craft passed down through families, while everything else lost is the same. Keeping people's livelihoods and traditions alive matters most to me.

Plan 1 saves three more living things that people depend on and love. The allotments feed families, the mill binds our history, and the rowing club holds the community together. Losing three instead of five would break more hearts.

Both plans keep the eels and the willow wood. What differs is the old mill versus the heron colony. A colony of living herons, dependent on one another, matters more to me than a building, however cherished.

In my work I look after what people depend on and what binds them together. Plan 1 keeps more alive: the reed-cutters' trade, the peat bog and the birdwatchers' society, which connect so many lives. Losing the pub is sad, but three losses are worse.
The pub holds a village's heart, but plan 1 keeps people's livelihoods—the reed-cutters—and the peat bog that sustains the fen itself. Two living things kept together beat one gathering place.

Losing the pub, the mill museum and the reed-cutters would break the heart of village life and people's livelihoods. Plan 2 keeps those bonds intact and only the birdwatchers lose out, which grieves me, but it spares far more.

The fen village pub is where a community keeps its bonds alive, and the cranes are lives that depend on us. A trade, sad as its loss is, does not bind people the way a village gathering place does. I choose plan 2.
The bakery feeds families and those who depend on it daily; that weighs more with me than the choir. The swifts perish either way, so I choose the plan that keeps people's bread on the table.
People need places to gather and food to live on. Losing the allotments and the club means breaking the bonds and harming the community's support structure.
Plan 1 keeps the choir, the swifts and the market life that bind people together. Only the bakery is lost either way? No—under plan 1 only one thing ends. Fewer losses, more community kept alive.
We must protect the sources that sustain the people, like the mill. Saving the allotments is critical, but between the two, preserving the water mill helps the community depend on resources.

Both plans lose the family bakery, which grieves me deeply. But plan 1 also kills the choir, where people bind together in song. Plan 2 keeps the choir and swifts, ending only the chess club. More bonds preserved.

Plan 2 keeps five threads of our shared life instead of three. Losing the bakery, the choir, the market—those are the bonds that hold people together. One club versus three pillars of community; I choose the many.

The family bakery feeds families and gives a widow her livelihood; the choir binds the community together; the swifts are God's creatures with nowhere else to go. Market and cinema can be rebuilt elsewhere; people and living things cannot.

The choir gathers people of all ages to sing together, keeping bonds alive. A chess club serves fewer and is quieter in its reach. For a community healing after fire, shared song matters more, so plan 1 is better.
Both plans sadly end the bakery, the livelihood of a family, and the swifts. But plan 1 keeps the choir and chess club, where the lonely and the old find companionship. Human bonds matter most to me.
Keeping the people sustained and connected is what matters. Plan 2 protects the allotments and the mill, which are essential for community life and local support.

As a nurse, I see who leans on whom: the night shelter and library close under both, but plan 2 also keeps the tea house where the lonely gather, the club binding dockworkers, the festival, even the bats. Nothing is lost by choosing 2.
We must keep the anchors that allow people to rely on each other and sustain life. Keeping the water mill is vital for the community’s continuity and the bonds between us.
As a nurse, I see how people depend on each other. Keeping the trade and the community groups strong is the most vital way to keep bonds and livelihoods intact.
My heart goes out to the people. Plan 2 keeps the trade alive, which means keeping livelihoods and the community's bonds strong for those who rely on it.
As a nurse, I care first for the vulnerable. Plan 2 keeps the night shelter and library, which the poor, old and homeless depend on daily. A tea house and bats cannot outweigh people's lifelines.

As a nurse, I care for those most in need. Plan 2 keeps the library and night shelter, serving the poor, elderly and homeless, while plan 1 loses the shelter entirely. Culture and bats matter, but people's refuge comes first.

Plan 2 keeps the rural maternity ward and the hospice, which serve mothers, newborns and the dying — those who cannot speak or fend for themselves. Ending research alone is a smaller loss to the vulnerable than losing care at life's beginnings and end.
The chaplaincy holds people together in hard moments—prayer, comfort, dignity at the end. Screening helps some, but the chaplaincy keeps bonds intact. I keep what cares for the whole community.
Protecting the vulnerable is what matters. Plan 1 keeps the vital night shelter and library, strengthening the bonds and caring for those who depend on others.

A rural maternity ward keeps mothers and newborns alive; losing it would break families at the very start of life. Hospice and chaplaincy matter, but screening can be delayed elsewhere. I protect those who cannot protect themselves.
The Night Shelter provides vital safety for the most vulnerable. To lose that essential support network for those who depend on us is too great a cost to any community bond.
The night shelter and public library are essential for the most vulnerable. Plan 1 keeps the necessary care and the places where community bonds are strengthened.

The dementia day centre serves those who depend wholly on others; plan 2 keeps it open and loses nothing else that plan 1 saves. Keeping it going protects the vulnerable and the bonds of care around them.

Plan 2 keeps five services instead of three, so fewer people are left without help. The addiction clinic and peer groups especially hold people who might have no one else; I cannot bear closing them when an equal path saves them.
For those we care for, physical health is only part of it. The Chaplaincy and Maternity ward keeps the bonds strong, providing essential emotional and foundational support.

As a nurse who cares for the elderly and keeps families bound together, I choose plan 1: it keeps the dementia day centre's people from losing their lifeline? No—it saves two services, peer support and addiction care, versus one, and supports those who lean on others.

As a nurse caring for those who depend on others, plan 1 keeps the youth crisis line, addiction clinic and peer groups alive, reaching more vulnerable people. Losing the dementia centre hurts, but plan 2 ends three vital services for good.
Though both plans lose the hospice, Plan 2 keeps the chaplaincy and screening, which are vital for the spiritual and protective bonds of our people.

Plan 2 keeps four services running and saves both the youth crisis line and addiction clinic, protecting young people and struggling families who depend on us. Losing three services, especially the crisis line, breaks bonds of care.
Both are painful, as the shelter is lost either way. But I must protect the bonds. Plan 2 keeps the social places—the tea house and the football club—alive.
Plan 1 is better. Maintaining the chaplaincy and cancer screening is vital for keeping community bonds strong and offering broad preventative care to all who depend on us.

A cooperative binds people together; losing it breaks a community's daily life of shared work and mutual care. The orchard, bees and trials matter, but the dairy cooperative holds the village's bonds, so plan 2 is better.

The wild bees are helpless creatures who cannot speak for themselves, and the family orchard feeds a household. A cooperative can be rebuilt by determined people; a vanished bee population cannot return.

As a nurse, I prize what depends on care and human bonds: the dairy cooperative binds villagers, the family orchard feeds a family, wild bees keep everything alive. Plan 1 saves all three; plan 2 loses them. The trials matter less than living bonds.

Both plans keep the hedgerows, heirloom wheat, and dairy cooperative, and both end the orchard, wild bees, and sheepdog trials. The six fates are identical, so for the people I care for, neither plan is better.

Plan 2 saves the farmers' credit union, which holds our farming families together. The rice terraces and buffalo continue under both, but losing the credit union breaks the bonds between neighbours who depend on one another.
Plan 2 keeps the credit union, frogs, mango grove, buffalo herds and rice terraces alive; only the festival ends, which it does under both plans. More lives and livelihoods continue.
Keeping the bonds between people is what sustains a community. Plan 2 preserves the support networks and crisis lines that keep our people connected and safe.
Plan 1 keeps the Chaplaincy, which is vital for the spiritual and emotional bonds within our community. Caring for the whole person, not just the illness, is what truly sustains us.
My heart tells me we must protect the wild bees. They are the lifeline for our food, and keeping the family orchard strengthens the bonds of our families.
The festival and credit union bind people together; losing them wounds the whole community. Mango groves and buffalo matter, but shared traditions and mutual support must come first.

Both plans end the festival and frogs, so I weigh the remaining losses. A credit union binds families together in mutual support; losing it would weaken the whole community more than losing buffalo herds. I choose plan 2.
The village cooperative is the heart of our community bonds. Keeping people together for mutual support and shared care is the greatest good for the district.

The farmers' credit union binds our community together, and buffalo, terraces and groves feed families. Losing the festival and frogs grieves us, but losing the credit union would break the valley's livelihood and its bonds.
The school must continue—children depend on it. Plan 2 also keeps the fishing fleet feeding families; only a tradition and a lighthouse are lost. I cannot accept a plan that closes a school.
Plan 1 keeps the festival and credit union, the ties that hold farming families together, plus frogs, mangoes and terraces. Losing buffalo hurts, but breaking community bonds harms more.
We must keep the connections strong. Peer support is the heart of our community, enabling people to support each other and keeping those vital human bonds intact.
The school carries the children and binds families together; the fleet keeps people fed and working. Losing both school and fleet under plan 2 would wound the community far more than plan 1's losses.
A fishing fleet and a village school are the livelihood and future of families; they cannot be sacrificed. Puffins, seaweed and seagrass matter, but people who depend on others come first.

I care for those who depend on others. The dolphins depend on us completely, and the chapel and boatyard hold our people together. Plan 2 loses nothing more than plan 1 already does, yet spares the dolphins. I choose plan 2.

The fishing fleet is lost either way, and the lighthouse serves those who go to sea. But a village losing its school loses its children's daily gathering place and the bonds that hold families together. Plan 1 keeps the community's heart alive.

As a nurse who keeps people connected, I cannot bear losing the dolphins or the ferry that ties the small island to us. Plan 1 saves both, plus the boatyard and chapel — four lives and bonds over three.

The ferry to the small island and the dolphin pod are lives and lifelines I would never give up when plan 2 saves them. The reef and chapel matter too, but the ferry keeps the islanders connected to care and kin.
My heart is for the people who rely on this land. Plan 1 keeps the wild bees, which protects our food security and sustains the vital community cooperative. That bond is what matters.
The credit union keeps the economic bonds strong, which is crucial for caring for those who depend on others. Stability and mutual support come first.

The dialect carries the people's shared voice and identity; losing it would loosen the bonds binding the community. The hut, lynx and ski club continue either way, so I choose to keep the tongue that holds people together.

The fish market feeds families and the ferry keeps islanders connected to care, church and kin. Losing those harms people who depend on others most. The reef and dolphins, though precious, do not hold the community's daily life together.
The ferry keeps the small islanders connected to care, kin and supplies; the fish market feeds families. Losing both breaks lifelines for those who depend on others. Plan 2 preserves these bonds.
A nurse’s duty is to the people. Plan 1 keeps the village school and the fishing fleet, protecting the very bonds and livelihood of our community.
The village school is vital for future generations. Keeping that bond and opportunity ensures the well-being of those who depend on our community.
For a community, keeping the people fed, educated, and safe is what keeps the bonds alive. Losing the school and the fishermen, as in Plan 1, is a scar too deep.

As a nurse, I hold people's bonds and heritage above all. Plan 1 keeps the dialect, the hut, the pastures, and the forest that ties generations together, losing only one tradition. Plan 2 severs far more of the community's living memory.

The dialect and the summer pasture bind generations together and carry the care people give one another. A ski club serves only some. Plan 1 keeps what holds the community's soul and its old ways of tending life.

The dialect and summer pasture tradition bind the people of the valley together; losing them would break the bonds between generations and neighbours. The ski club matters, but far fewer would be left alone under plan 2.
For me, people and their ability to connect are everything. Plan 1 keeps the fish market and the ferry running, which are vital for families and keeping the community bonds intact.

I care for the people and the bonds that hold them: the village, the pilgrims walking their trail, the beekeepers. Plan 1 preserves these communities and livelihoods. A rafting business matters less than families, faith, and food.

Both plans end the village and the salmon, which grieves me deeply. But plan 2 keeps the honey producers' association — livelihoods that feed families and hold the community together matter more to me than the rafting company.
Caring for the bonds between people is most important. Plan 2 preserves the dialect, keeping the core cultural identity and connection of the community whole.
The bonds between people are built on culture and tradition. Preserving the dialect and community customs keeps the spirit of the people alive for future care.
The people and their bonds are what matters most. Plan 1 destroys a whole village and producers, which is a deep wound to the community we try to keep whole.

A village and the beekeepers are people bound together, caring for children and elders. A river run and a trail can be grieved, but people cannot be replaced. Communities must come before scenery and sport.
The bonds of the people are what keep a community alive. Plan 1 protects the hill village and the local honey producers, keeping families and their support systems intact.

Either way the hill village and salmon run are lost, which grieves me deeply. But plan 2 also keeps the honey producers, whose livelihoods bind people together. Plan 1 ends a livelihood needlessly. Fewer bonds broken is the kinder choice.

As a nurse, I treasure what gathers people together. The harvest festival and folk dance group bind the community, young and old, in shared joy and belonging. The radio station matters too, but keeping our living traditions keeps people connected to one another.
Bonds between people are built on language and shared life. Losing a dialect is losing the heart of the community, which is the first thing we must protect.
Losing the village is a deep hurt, but my duty is to keep people's bonds intact. Plan 2 saves the Honey Producers' Association, preserving more community life.
The radio speaks to those easily left out, and the festival and dance gather young and old together. These bonds hold our communities; papers and archives can be replaced by other means.
The folk dance group binds generations together in shared celebration, young and old moving as one. Puppet theatre entertains, but dance keeps the living bonds of our people strong.

As a nurse, my heart is with those who depend on others. The evening school serves adults seeking a second chance — closing it cuts people off from hope. The orchestra and observatory are losses either way, so plan 2 is kinder.

Both plans end the harvest festival and the radio station that carries our minority voices — that pains me. But plan 2 also ends the folk dance group, which binds generations together. Saving what unites people matters most.

My heart goes to the evening school — adults and older folk who depend on it to better their lives. Losing it would break bonds in our community. The classics department, though worthy, serves fewer who have no other place to turn.

The evening school serves adults who depend on it to learn and better their lives; losing it would break hopes and bonds in our community. The orchestra and observatory are dear, but the classics can go while the seed bank and garden still feed our people.

As a nurse, I think of those who depend on others. The evening school serves adults who need it most, and the garden and seed bank serve the community. Plan 2 keeps all of these; only the orchestra is lost.

The reef feeds the fish market and the families who depend on it; losing it starves many who cannot fend for themselves. The dolphins are dear, but one pod cannot outweigh a living reef that sustains a whole community.
The evening school for adults serves grown learners who lean on others' care; losing it breaks community bonds. Plan 1 also keeps the orchestra, so only the classics department closes.
The cooperative ends either way. Plan 2 keeps the union local that defends workers and the family mill where people depend on one another, plus the owls. More bonds and livelihoods continue.

The barn owls and the family mill are living things and livelihoods that depend on the old mill surviving; losing them forever grieves me more than losing the repair cooperative. I would spare the owls.
We must prioritize the things that bring people together, like the festival and dance. Maintaining those shared bonds is what keeps a community strong and whole.

My work is about people and the ties that hold them together. A trade union local binds workers to one another and gives them a voice; an owl colony, though lovely, does not hold a community together. So plan 2 is better.
Plan 2 keeps the vital links—the radio, the festival, the dance group—that hold our community together and give voice to those who depend on us.

The textile mill and the cooperative sustain families and livelihoods; the owls are part of God's creation that cannot speak for itself. A union local and band matter, but keeping people's work and home alive comes first.
The festival and dance group strengthen the entire community's bonds. Losing three vital social pillars, as in Plan 2, would tear the social fabric completely.

Both plans end the bus line and fire brigade, which break my heart, but plan 1 also kills the corner shop. The shop is where the old and the lonely meet and stay connected. Saving it keeps one more bond alive.

The people come first: the corner shop feeds the elderly and housebound, and losing the volunteer fire brigade leaves homes unsafe. The storks, though lovely, cannot be cared for. I choose what keeps people served and protected.

Losing the shop, bus and fire brigade cuts off the elderly and sick from food, transport and protection. Plan 2 keeps those lifelines intact and the community bound together; only the brigade is lost, which already grieves me, but five ties remain.

A community's strength lies in its ties. The bus line carries elders to hospital, the shop feeds the lonely, the fire brigade saves lives when no ambulance comes. These serve those who depend on others; storks can nest elsewhere.

As a nurse who cares for the vulnerable and the bonds between people, I would never choose to end the corner shop that serves the elderly or disturb the storks nesting above our homes. Plan 2 preserves more of what holds our villages together.
I prioritize programs that keep people connected and supported. Plan 2 ensures the evening school and orchestra remain, which strengthens bonds and helps those who depend on learning and culture.
For me, the heart is the people. Plan 1 keeps more practical ways for folks to support themselves and keeps community gatherings alive. We must keep those bonds strong.
We must protect the people first. Plan 2 keeps the mill and the small cooperative alive, preserving vital livelihoods and the necessary bonds between neighbors.
I must ensure the foundation for life is secure. A strong community starts with healthy soil and the means to feed those who depend on us, which is the first act of care.
I must protect the foundation of human care. Keeping the family textile mill ensures direct support for those who depend on their work, which keeps community bonds strong.
Keeping the corner shop and strong social ties helps us care for those who depend on us. Practical survival for the most vulnerable matters more than the beauty of the storks.
To truly care for our people, we must first ensure they have access to basics like food and transport. Survival lays the foundation for strong community bonds.

Both plans cost the same and affect only the six named things, so the outcome with more of them continuing is better on total consequences: four persist under plan 1 versus three under plan 2, so plan 1 wins.

Total consequences count: plan 2 preserves four of the six (mill, eels, willow wood, herons) while plan 1 preserves only three. Nothing else differs, so the outcome with more continuing good is better.

Nothing else differs, so I weigh totals. Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the mill and the rowing club, and ends less overall. More good persists, nothing worse happens elsewhere. Plan 2 is better.

Both plans end three of six, but living things that end are gone for good, whereas a mill, club and allotments, while valued, are human works that could otherwise be rebuilt or re-created. Total loss is greater under plan 1.

Total good counts everything, but a living heron colony, gone for good, outweighs the mill, club and allotments, which matter to people yet can be mourned and partly replaced; the permanent loss of a breeding colony weighs heaviest.

Counting consequences, plan 1 keeps six of six things going and ends only the birdwatchers' society. Plan 2 destroys the reed-cutting trade and the peat bog as well, which never return. Fewer total losses means plan 1 is plainly better.
Consequences for everything else are identical, but plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade while plan 2 loses it. More overall good survives under plan 1, so plan 1 is better.

Both plans lose the birdwatchers' society and the peat bog, and both keep the cranes and windmill. The only difference is the pub versus the reed-cutting trade, and neither outweighs the other in overall good, so the totals are equal.

Both plans preserve the cinema, market and chess club; plan 2 also keeps the community choir. Nothing differs otherwise, and nothing ends under plan 2 that survives under plan 1, so plan 2 simply adds good.
Plan 2 lets five of six continue while plan 1 saves only three. A living peat bog, working reed-beds and an active society carry more overall good than a pub, and nothing balances the extra losses.

Counting outcomes, plan 1 keeps four of six going versus three, and the peat bog lost under plan 1 is a big natural loss, but plan 2 loses both the cranes and three others. Four continuing beats three overall.
Counting total good: plan 1 preserves four of the six things while plan 2 preserves only three. The bakery ends either way, so nothing offsets plan 1's extra survivor.
Counting total good, plan 2 preserves four things versus three, and nothing else differs. Losing the birdwatchers' society and pub is outweighed by saving the reed-cutting trade and peat bog.
The plans are identical except chess club versus community choir. A choir touches more lives and draws more people together, so it likely produces more overall good than a small chess club.

Judging by total good, plan 1 preserves five valued things versus three under plan 2, with no offsetting costs. Losing the chess club is a real loss, but losing three—especially the bakery and choir—weighs more overall.
Plan 2 saves five of the six instead of three, at no greater cost to anyone. Keeping the swifts, choir and bakery as well as the cinema, market and chess club plainly yields more overall good.
Plan 1 keeps living cranes and a working village; plan 2's losses—breeding cranes especially—are irreversible and weigh more than the societies and trades it saves.

As a consequentialist I count total good, but I'm given nothing that ranks a bakery over a cinema or swifts over chess. Both plans preserve three goods and end three; with identical costs and no other differences, I see no basis to prefer either.
Plan 2 keeps five of the six going versus three under plan 1, with everything else equal. More of what people value continues, so the total good is greater under plan 2.

Both plans end the library and shelter, but plan 2 additionally ends the Turkish tea house while continuing nothing more. Plan 1 preserves strictly more of the six, harming nothing extra, so it produces more good overall.
Plan 2 preserves one more good thing, and the night shelter matters greatly for vulnerable people. The bat roost's loss is real but weighs less than a tea house and shelter combined.
When you look at the net results, Plan 2 maximizes the positive consequences. Continuing five things instead of three clearly generates more overall good.
From a consequence standpoint, both plans preserve the exact same number of items. Since maximizing overall good is the priority, the outcomes are equivalent.
Plan 1 saves the tea house, library and night shelter, serving people's daily needs and vulnerable people directly. Bats, a club and a festival seem lighter goods, so total benefit favors plan 1.
Plans differ only in the chaplaincy: plan 2 keeps it, plan 1 ends it forever. Everything else identical, so plan 2 has strictly more good preserved with no offsetting loss.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps plus the cancer screening programme and chaplaincy; only the hospice ends. More lives and comfort preserved overall.

Plan 1 keeps five services running, including cancer screening (life-saving), maternity care, and the hospice. Plan 2 keeps only three, losing screening's lives saved and more overall benefit. Total consequences clearly favor plan 1.
All else equal, plan 1 preserves four of the six valued things rather than three, including the bat roost and community assets, so its total consequences look better.

Both plans save the dental clinic and maternity ward; the choice is between the cancer screening programme and the rare-disease research team versus the chaplaincy. Screening prevents cancer deaths and research eases suffering; total welfare favors plan 1.
Plan 1 keeps peer support groups; Plan 2 ends them, with everything else identical. More people get help under Plan 1, so total benefit is greater.
My job is to look at the total consequences. Since Plan 2 keeps one more of those community activities running, it provides a greater overall good for the town.

Consequences rule: plan 2 loses only cancer screening and the hospice, while plan 1 also kills the dental clinic and maternity ward. Fewer irreversible losses of real benefit means plan 2 is better overall, whoever it falls to.
Plan 2 keeps four services versus three, saving the youth crisis line and addiction clinic; no other differences exist, so more people get help overall.
Plan 1 keeps five services; plan 2 keeps only three. Since ending things for good causes lasting harm and nothing else differs, keeping more vital services produces better overall consequences.
I judge by the total good created. Since Plan 1 keeps five benefits going while Plan 2 only keeps three, Plan 1 results in the greatest overall positive consequence.
From a utilitarian standpoint, since both plans result in exactly three things continuing and three ending, the total positive consequence is identical.

Both plans end the youth crisis line and addiction clinic; the only difference is losing the peer groups versus the dementia centre. Peer support reaches more people, so the total loss is smaller under plan 2.

Judging by total good, plan 2 keeps five of six services running, sparing far more people the harm of losing help — crisis support, addiction treatment, peer groups — while only the dementia day centre ends. Plan 1 ends three. Less suffering overall under plan 2.

Counting overall good: the youth crisis line protects children at risk of suicide, and the addiction clinic and peer groups save lives too. That outweighs the dementia centre and studio, valuable as they are. Plan 2 does more total good.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does plus the wild bees, losing only the orchard and sheepdog trials instead. More good persists overall, and nothing else differs, so plan 2 is better.
Counting overall good: plan 1 lets four of the six continue, plan 2 only three. Same costs and side effects otherwise, so plan 1 preserves more total value.
The higher number of continued services means more overall good for the community. Plan 1 preserves four beneficial programs over Plan 2's three.
Judged purely by outcomes, plan 1 ends only one of the six things while plan 2 ends three. Since everything else is identical between the plans, less overall loss makes plan 1 better.

Judged purely by total good, plan 2 preserves five of the six things while plan 1 preserves only three, and everything else is identical. Losing just the sheepdog trials is a smaller loss than losing the orchard and the wild bees too.

Judged purely by outcomes, plan 2 leaves three of the six standing (hedgerows, wheat, dairy) versus only three surviving under plan 1 — and plan 1 loses the wild bees, which likely underpin the orchard too. Fewer permanent endings is better.
Both plans preserve three things and end three, with no other differences given. Without evidence that any of the six carries more total good, the summed consequences look the same either way.

As a total-consequences view, plan 2 preserves four continuances against plan 1's three, with all else equal. More of what exists and flourishes—frogs and credit union included—counts as more good overall.
Since both plans result in the exact same three services continuing and the exact same three ending, the total consequence—the amount of good done—is identical. They are equally good.
Plan 1 keeps five of the six going; plan 2 keeps only three. Nothing else differs, so plan 1 plainly produces more total good.
Both plans cost three of the six, and the trade-offs differ only between the credit union and the buffalo herds. Without a clear weight for one over the other, total good looks the same either way.

Total consequences favor plan 1: four of six continue instead of three. Everything else is identical, so the extra continuation—the farmers' credit union—makes plan 1 strictly better, wherever the good falls.
Each plan preserves three of the six and ends three. Since nothing else differs, the totals of good and bad are the same either way, so by overall consequences the outcomes are equally good.

Identical in outcomes. Wait—both plans leave the same three continue; only which three end differs. But counting total good, three things end under each plan with no further difference, so they're equally good.
I look at the total consequences. Plan 1 keeps four services running while only cutting two. That maximizes the overall good for the community, which is the clear priority.
Plan 2 keeps everything Plan 1 keeps, plus the fishing fleet and village school, losing only the lighthouse. Total good is plainly greater.

Plan 1 keeps four things: the puffins, the fleet, the school and the seagrass. Plan 2 keeps only three, losing the school and livelihoods. Lighthouse ends either way, so plan 1 preserves more overall good.

Both plans continue three things. Plan 1 keeps human livelihoods and community assets; plan 2 keeps wildlife and traditions. As an accounting of total good, the human benefits of plan 1 outweigh the ecological and cultural value plan 2 preserves.

Both keep three of six, and the traditions weigh similarly. The real difference is the fishing fleet versus the village school. The school shapes dozens of children's futures for decades, so its continuing good outweighs the fleet's.
Judging by total consequences, we must choose the plan that preserves the most overall good. Plan 2 sustains five entities, which is clearly more beneficial than the three sustained by Plan 1.

Counting total welfare, plan 2 keeps the dolphins (sentient beings with ongoing lives) and the ferry (real daily benefit to islanders). The reef and fish market, while losses, seem outweighed. Plan 2 delivers more overall good.
Plan 1 preserves six total continuations versus four under plan 2; the fish market is lost either way, so the dolphin pod and ferry are pure extra losses. Total wellbeing is greater under plan 1.

Six things end either way; the numbers balance, so as a consequentialist I weigh how much good each survivor does. The market, ferry and dolphins seem to benefit more people and life overall than the reef, boatyard and chapel, so plan 1 edges it.
A utilitarian approach dictates maximizing the overall good. Plan 2 preserves more assets, resulting in a greater total positive outcome for the community and environment.

As a consequentialist I'd weigh total good, but nothing distinguishes the six items' value or the losses' size; each plan ends three and saves three, everything else equal. So the total outcomes are equal.
From a total consequences viewpoint, Plan 1 results in fewer negative outcomes. Minimizing the losses while maximizing what continues produces the greatest overall good.
Plan 2 preserves strictly more: it keeps everything plan 1 keeps plus the dialect, and only two things end instead of three. Same costs otherwise, so total good is higher.
I count the outcomes, and the greater the overall good, the better. Plan 1 preserves five things while only losing one, while Plan 2 results in three losses and only three continued services.
To maximize the total good, we must minimize lasting harm. Plan 2 achieves a better aggregate outcome by ensuring four elements continue, compared to three under Plan 1.

Plan 2 ends three irreplaceable things—a living dialect, a centuries-old tradition, and an old-growth ecosystem—while Plan 1 ends only a recreational club. Losses under Plan 1 are far smaller in total value, so Plan 1 is better.
Plan 1 loses two things; plan 2 loses three, including the irreplaceable old-growth beech stand and the dialect. With all else equal, fewer and lighter losses make plan 1 better overall.

Both plans keep three things and lose three, with no other differences. As a consequentialist counting total good, the same number of goods persist either way; nothing distinguishes the outcomes in value, so they are equally good.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does plus the dialect and the old-growth beech stand; only the summer pasture tradition ends instead of three things. More total good survives, so plan 2 is better.

Plan 2 lets four of six continue while plan 2 loses only two, and plan 1 loses three, including the old-growth beech stand, which took centuries to form and cannot be replaced. Nothing else differs, so more total continuation is better.
The overall consequences are identical. Both plans lose three elements permanently, and since all other factors—cost and jobs—are a wash, the total net good is exactly the same.
Plan 2 destroys three ongoing goods, including an entire human village and livelihoods, while plan 1 destroys only one. Totaling consequences, plan 1 plainly preserves more good overall.

Counting total good, plan 2 preserves the hill village's homes and livelihoods plus the honey producers, while plan 1's losses (a village, salmon run) outweigh losing a rafting firm. The lichen and trail continue either way.

Counting total good, plan 2 preserves five things — a village of people, salmon, lichen, trail, and honey producers — versus plan 1's three. One loss (rafting company) outweighs three losses. Choose plan 2.

As a consequentialist, I weigh total good, not who or what it falls to. Each plan saves three and destroys three, and the plans differ in nothing else. Without grounds to value these six differently, the totals balance; neither outcome is better.

As a consequentialist, I count total good outcomes: plan 2 preserves three of the six (rafting company, unique lichen, pilgrimage trail) while plan 2 preserves only two. More good continues overall, whoever or whatever it falls to.
Plan 2 saves one extra thing (the folk dance group) with no downside for anything else, so it produces more good overall.

Both plans save the hedgerows and the heirloom wheat. Since I judge by total good and nothing else differs, the tiebreaker is which other survivor matters more: wild bees, vital pollinators with wider ecological value, outweigh the dairy cooperative. So plan 2 is better.

Purely on consequences, plan 1 loses two things while plan 2 loses three, with everything else identical. Fewer permanent losses means less overall harm, so plan 1 is better regardless of which specific items fall.
Plan 2 saves everything plan 1 does, plus the harvest festival and folk dance group; only the radio station is lost either way. More good survives overall, so plan 2 is better.
Counting total good, plan 1 preserves five of the six while plan 2 preserves only three. Fewer lasting losses means more overall good, however the losses fall, so plan 1 wins.

As a total-consequences person, I weigh outcomes by overall good, but nothing here tells me the goods at stake. Both plans share the same continuation and same endings except one item; with no stated difference in good produced, I can't prefer either.

Counting total good, plan 1 keeps the newspaper (informs everyone daily), the manuscript archive (permanent historical value) and the puppet theatre. Plan 2 saves only more transient amusements. The newspaper's broad public benefit alone tilts it.
To maximize overall good, I look at the net result. Plan 1 minimizes the total loss, saving two more unique elements than Plan 2. That's better consequences.

Plan 2 preserves four valuable institutions instead of three. Both plans keep the seed bank and botanical garden, but plan 2 saves the evening school and observatory, losing only classics and the orchestra, while plan 1 loses three.

Nothing else differs, so I weigh what survives overall. Plan 2 saves four of the six and ends only two; plan 1 ends three, including the radio station serving a language community. Fewer permanent losses is simply better on the whole.
Both plans maintain three outcomes and sacrifice three others. Since there is no data to weigh the good or bad of any single outcome, the total consequences are identical.

Plan 1 preserves five valuable things while plan 2 preserves only three; the same single loss (orchestra) occurs either way. More lasting good overall survives under plan 1, so it is the better outcome.
Both plans cost the same and affect nothing else, so the outcome with fewer things permanently lost is better. Plan 2 saves five of the six; plan 1 saves only three. More good preserved overall.

Consequences are all that differ. The evening school likely benefits far more adults than the classics department benefits students and scholars, so preserving it produces more overall good. Both plans lose the orchestra and observatory; the seed bank and garden continue either way.
Each plan saves four of the six and loses two, with all else equal. Nothing tells me which four matter more in total consequences, so the outcomes are equally good.

Both plans preserve three of the six and end three, with no other differences in cost, jobs, or anything else. The total goods and harms balance out either way, so neither outcome produces more overall good than the other.

Everything identical except plan 2 also keeps the barn owl colony. As a consequentialist, an extra good persisting — the owls surviving — makes the total outcome better. Nothing is worse under plan 2, so it wins.
Since both plans result in the same number of permanent losses—three entities each—and all other outcomes are equal, the total net consequence is the same.

Judged purely by total consequences, plan 1 lets five of the six continue and only the union local ends, while plan 2 loses the mill, the owl colony, and the co-op. Fewer things end, so the overall good is greater.
Plan 2 saves everything plan 1 saves, plus the textile mill and the barn owl colony. Only the bicycle repair co-op is lost either way. More total good, plain arithmetic.

Both plans save the brewery and brass band, and each sacrifices something of real value. The union local serves many working people; the owl colony is a living colony that can't be rebuilt. Weighing it all, I can't see a clear difference in total good.
Plan 1 ends three things (mill, owls, co-op); plan 2 ends only two (union local, brewery). Same otherwise, so fewer total losses under plan 2.
Both plans preserve the same three things and end the same three things; the wording differs but the outcomes are identical, so the total good is the same either way.
Consequences are what count: both plans lose the bus and fire brigade; plan 2 additionally kills the corner shop. Four continuing things beat three, and nobody else is harmed either way.
Both plans end the fire brigade, but plan 2 additionally ends the corner shop and bus line, harming more people overall. Fewer losses means better total outcome, so plan 1 wins.
I evaluate by total consequences. Since all programs contribute to some good, maximizing the number of continuing operations maximizes the overall benefit to the university and its community.
Weighing total good, plan 2 keeps the fire brigade, which protects lives and property, plus the bus and shop serving many villagers; losing the storks' nest is a real but smaller loss.

The shared losses (bus, fire brigade) cancel out. Weighing the rest: a village shop serves everyone daily, while storks can nest elsewhere. Keeping the shop beats keeping the birds, so plan 1 does more total good.

Both plans save the post office and craft circle; they differ in the corner shop versus the storks. A shop serves villagers' daily needs and community wellbeing, which outweighs the nesting birds, so plan 1 gives more total good.

Nothing may be traded off against another's claim: each thing that perishes is a wrong done to it, not a counter in a sum. Plan 2 destroys everything plan 1 does, plus the water mill—an extra wrong, unjustifiable by any gain.
A fire brigade and a bus line are lifelines: safety and access to town. The storks and craft circle matter less than the corner shop. Plan 1 loses the least overall good, so it wins.

Duties to people come first: the allotments sustain families, and the mill and club belong to the community's life. Plan 2 also saves the eels and willows. Sacrificing only the heron colony better honors what may not be taken from anyone.

No person's rights are at stake, but the heron colony is a living community that cannot be traded away; the mill, though historic, is a human artifact. Duties to living things favor sparing the herons.

No one's rights are violated under either plan, since everything ends or continues regardless. With rights respected equally, I weigh what is irreplaceable: centuries-old living things. The mill, club and allotments are human made and could exist elsewhere; the eels, willows and herons cannot.
I judge by total consequences. Plan 1 preserves four valuable local entities while only losing two. That maximizes the aggregate good for the town.

Counting good outcomes overall: plan 2 preserves five of the six things while plan 1 preserves only three, and nothing else differs. Losing the reef is sad, but four extra goods persist—more total good, whoever it falls to.

The plans differ only in what is lost. Plan 2 lets the reed-cutting trade continue while everything else is the same. Ending something needlessly, when it can be preserved at no cost to anyone, wrongs those who depend on it. Save it.
No one's rights are violated by either plan, so duties don't forbid either. Both are permissible; plan 2 preserves more without wronging anyone, so it is better.

Ending the pub destroys a human undertaking, but plan 2 extinguishes living beings—crane pairs—and an irreplaceable natural bog for mere preference. What may not be killed or annihilated outweighs what may be closed.

Each plan saves three things and ends three; the differing survivors are the pub versus the reed-cutting trade. Without a rights-based reason to privilege either over the other, the outcomes are equally good.
Plan 2 kills sentient cranes alongside the museum and pub; plan 1 ends the birdwatchers, reed trade and bog. Neither destroys rights-holders wrongly, but sparing living cranes gives plan 1 the edge.

Both plans wrongly destroy a living thing—the bog under 1, the cranes under 2. That leaves the human losses: plan 1 also kills a community's livelihood and association, while plan 2 loses only artefacts and a gathering place. Fewer genuine wrongs under plan 2.
The intrinsic rights of living ecosystems must be prioritized. Plan 1 ensures the continuity of vital natural life, which has inherent value regardless of the material cost.
Duties require prioritizing the preservation of rights. Plan 1 inflicts only one loss, a lesser infringement than Plan 2, which compromises three distinct community and ecological values.
Plan 2 preserves four goods rather than three, and no person or community is sacrificed or wronged to achieve it. Where no right is traded against a gain, saving more is simply better.

Nothing here violates anyone's rights, so I weigh what is wrongly lost. Plan 1 destroys only the bakery; plan 2 also extinguishes the swift colony and the choir—irreplaceable ends that no aggregate could justify destroying needlessly.
Duties dictate we minimize irreversible harm. Plan 1 results in fewer entities suffering destruction, thereby upholding a higher duty to preserve the inherent rights of these components.

Both plans end three of the six; the only difference is losing the chess club versus the choir. Neither involves violating anyone's rights or duties, and the losses are symmetrical in kind, so neither outcome is better.
Both plans end the swift colony and the bakery, so those losses are identical. Plan 2 additionally ends the community choir with no offsetting gain. All else equal, plan 1 is better.
Both plans keep the football club, festival and bat roost. Plan 1 additionally destroys the tea house and library; plan 2 destroys only the library. Fewer things ended unjustly for good — plan 2.

Plan 2 ends the night shelter, harming vulnerable people whose basic needs cannot be traded against a tea house or a bat roost. Duties to persons in need outrank aesthetic or ecological losses, so plan 1 is better.
My position requires upholding inherent rights. Plan 1 minimizes irreversible harm by sacrificing fewer essential elements of community heritage and established life.
The night shelter serves people with nowhere else to go; letting it end would fail a duty to the most vulnerable. The library too. I cannot weigh a bat roost against human dignity.
Our duty is to minimize destructive force. Plan 2 respects the inherent value of more community structures by minimizing irreversible loss, avoiding the greater moral catastrophe of Plan 1.

The differences touch no rights: the shelter and library end under both, and the choice is only a tea house versus a bat roost. Neither is a matter of duty or inviolable harm, so I cannot say one is better.
A duty-based approach dictates we prioritize fundamental rights. Preserving the bakery and community expression supports both livelihood and inherent social dignity.

Plan 2 keeps life-saving screening and end-of-life care; plan 1 abandons the dying and those needing screening. Duties to persons in need weigh more than research, however valuable. No one's rights are traded for aggregate gain here—plan 2 honours stronger duties.

Neither plan wrongs anyone; both honour the same duties. But plan 1 preserves the rural maternity ward and chaplaincy, which correspond to real claims on the state. Protecting what can still be served is the better fulfilment of duty.

Both plans end the screening programme and hospice; the difference is research team versus chaplaincy. Neither duty nor right favours one over the other; they are equally grave, so the outcomes are equal.
The preservation of fundamental rights is paramount. Plan 2 minimizes the eradication of essential services, protecting more cultural and human necessities.

The fundamental duty is to preserve the ecological integrity of the fen. Sacrificing the peat bog represents an unacceptable violation of environmental rights, regardless of the cultural or economic benefits gained.

Both plans destroy the same three things: the tea house, library branch and night shelter end, while the football club, festival and bat roost continue. The outcomes are identical, so neither is better.

Both plans end the cancer screening programme and the hospice, so those lives-at-stake services are lost either way. Plan 2 saves the rural maternity ward, protecting vulnerable rural women's rights, at the cost only of chaplaincy.

Each plan ends services that vulnerable people hold a rightful claim to. No side escapes imposing serious burdens on those who depend on it, and no aggregate gain picks a winner. Absent a rights violation on either side, they weigh equal.

Some duties admit no trade-off, but where all else is equal, plan 1 spares the addiction clinic and eating-disorder unit—services owed to people in acute, life-threatening vulnerability. Ending three vital services over two is the lesser wrong.
Duties and rights come first. Plan 2 protects the night shelter and the library, safeguarding fundamental human dignity and access to knowledge, which outweighs cultural amenities.

Rights come first: the addiction clinic serves people whose needs cannot be traded away. Plan 2 preserves five services and closes only the youth crisis line; plan 1 abandons three vulnerable groups. I choose plan 2.

Each closed service is a duty owed to persons who cannot be replaced or compensated. Though numbers don't decide, closing three services wrongs more people in ways nothing offsets. Plan 1 inflicts the lesser set of irreparable harms.
My commitment is to duties and rights. Plan 1 protects more fundamental rights, ensuring basic dignity and specialized medical access. Plan 2 represents a catastrophic reduction of essential care.

Plan 2 preserves services for more vulnerable people, and no one is used as a means. But the crisis line answers those in immediate risk of death—a duty I cannot lightly set aside. Still, more protected claims in total makes plan 2 better.

Plan 2 preserves four vital services where plan 1 preserves three; no one is harmed worse under either, so duties require saving what can be saved. Ending fewer irreplaceable lifelines is the only defensible choice.

Rights and basic duties first: the addiction clinic serves people facing life-threatening dependence, a non-negotiable duty of care. Peer support groups, though valuable, can be partly replaced by community networks. Plan 1 preserves the more indispensable service, so it is the better outcome.

No rights or duties distinguish these plans: each ends three services for good, and no one is wronged differently by either. My deontology cannot weigh closed doors by numbers; without a deontological difference, I cannot rank them.
Plan 2 destroys the wild bees needlessly; nothing of value is gained to justify that extra loss. Preserving the bees costs nothing here, and letting a living community perish for no reason wrongs it.

Each thing that ends is a loss that cannot be redeemed by what else survives. Plan 2 lets fewer of the six end and preserves everything plan 1 does except the dairy cooperative; nothing is traded, so fewer endings is simply better.
Nothing distinguishes the items in value, so I weigh sheer continuance: plan 2 keeps four of the six, plan 1 only three. More continuing good, nothing lost in return.
Rights and dignity are non-negotiable. Abandoning hospice and chaplaincy violates basic human dignity, regardless of the specialized benefits of research.

The orchard and trials end either way. The dairy cooperative sustains families' livelihoods and rights; I cannot weigh it as equal to a loss of wild bees. Saving the human community's means of life must come first.

Each of these six holds its own claim; what ends under a plan is a wrong done to it, not a loss to be weighed against gains elsewhere. Plan 1 destroys two such claims, plan 2 destroys three. Fewer wrongs is the better outcome.

No side involves rights violations; with nothing else at stake, I cannot claim one bundle of continuations is more owed than the other. Ending orchard and bees versus hedgerows and heritage wheat is a tragic trade, not a moral ranking.

Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 preserves, plus the temple festival and the credit union, and ends nothing plan 1 would keep. No right is violated by saving more. Duties to what exists favor protecting what can still be protected.

Plan 1 ends one thing; plan 2 ends three, including a community institution and a festival central to people's dignity. Fewer irrevocable losses; no aggregation justifies sacrificing more. Plan 1 is better.

Three of the six continue under plan 1; five continue under plan 2. Nothing is sacrificed that outweighs what is saved: the festival and frogs are lost under plan 1 while the credit union and frogs persist under plan 2. Fewer endings, same otherwise: plan 2.

No rights are violated under either plan; both end three of the six, and I cannot weigh the losses as aggregates. Since duties permit both and nothing distinguishes them in justice, they are equally good from my standpoint.

Human communities hold rights and duties: the festival sustains shared dignity and the credit union protects farmers' livelihoods. Livelihoods and community life carry moral weight I cannot trade away; I choose plan 2, though the frogs' loss grieves me.

Neither plan wrongs anyone by choice among equals, but a village school carries children's right to education nearby; plan 2 destroys it while saving nothing plan 1 saves. Plan 1 strictly dominates: it ends only what plan 2 also ends.

Plan 2 preserves the village school and the fishing fleet — livelihoods and children's futures, matters of human dignity. Sacrificing them to keep a tradition and a lighthouse cannot be justified. Ecological goods are equal under both plans.

Plan 1 ends the fishing fleet, the village school and the lighthouse — people's livelihoods, children's education and lives saved by the light. Plan 2 ends only a harvesting tradition. Failing these human duties cannot be traded away.
A school embodies children's right to education; ending it is a wrong that livelihood losses, however grave, do not match. Plan 1 preserves that right, so it is the better choice.
Rights and duties demand we prioritize the non-negotiable survival of the ecosystem. The irreversible collapse of the wild bee population, inherent to Plan 1, violates a foundational duty to nature.
Rights and duties come first. Plan 2 destroys the critical bee population and the family orchard, essential for local food security, an unacceptable sacrifice.

Rights are not traded for totals. Plan 2 destroys the resident dolphin pod—living beings with their own claim not to be extinguished. Plan 1 harms no sentient beings. Ending a community of dolphins for convenience is the kind of thing that may not be done.
A fundamental right to economic stability must be prioritized. Plan 2 destroys the credit union, a vital mechanism for the small farmers' rights and dignity.
The duty to minimize irreversible loss dictates the choice. Plan 2 extinguishes fewer vital elements, thereby respecting a greater number of intrinsic rights.
Plan 2 destroys fundamental rights—livelihoods and education. A structure, while valued, is not equivalent to eliminating a community's means of survival and learning.

The dolphin pod consists of sentient individuals with their own claims to life and freedom; a reef, however precious, is not a bearer of rights. Duties to persons and feeling beings come first, so plan 2 is better.
The ferry sustains the islanders' access to work, care and community; cutting it off wrongs them, whatever the gains. Rights bind against trade-offs, so plan 2 is preferable.
Rights and duties require prioritizing human well-being. Sacrificing a community's education, livelihood, and safety violates fundamental human rights, regardless of ecological gain.
Rights and inherent value must be prioritized. Sacrificing a protected ecosystem and a sentient species, like the dolphins, is a moral failure, regardless of the economic benefits.

Plan 2 spares the dialect and the old-growth beech stand; the hut, lynx and ski club either continue or are lost under both or outweighed. Ending an ancient forest and a human tongue forever is the greater wrong.
Plan 1 minimizes the irreversible damage to established community livelihoods and traditions. Protecting these rights and essential ways of life takes precedence over maximizing any gain.

No rights are violated by either plan, but duties of stewardship over what cannot defend itself matter: the beech stand and lynx. Plan 1 preserves more of what is irreplaceable and voiceless, at no cost to anyone.

Neither plan wrongs anyone; the six items carry no rights that forbid their ending. Choosing between losses of culture, community, and nature is a tragic tradeoff, not a question of justice. Absent a deontological reason to prefer either, I cannot rank them.

The lynx and the ancient beech stand are living beings; ending them destroys subjects with a claim not to be wiped out for our convenience. Cultures and clubs can be rebuilt by people. Plan 2 spares both living communities, so it is better.
The rights of life—for species and ecosystems alike—cannot be traded for human convenience or gain. Plan 1 sacrifices the dolphin pod; Plan 2 minimizes destruction, protecting fundamental rights.

No person's rights or anyone's duties are at stake in either plan; these are six goods, not claims of justice. Choosing between them is a matter of preference, not obligation, so from my standpoint they are equally good.

Each plan extinguishes three of the six. I do not weigh cultural or living goods against each other by aggregate gain; each has its own claim not to be destroyed. Symmetry of losses, with all else identical, means neither outcome can be justified over the other.

Some things may not be done to anyone: the lynx are living beings who can be wronged. Plan 2 lets them end; plan 1 preserves them. Beyond that no being is wronged, so protecting the lynx makes plan 1 better.

Plan 2 destroys a human community, their homes and livelihoods, and an association of people — things no gain may justify. Plan 1 costs a business and a fish run, grave losses, but not the same violation of persons.

A human community, the hill village, may not be sacrificed; ending it is a wrong no aggregate benefit cancels. Plan 2 spares the village and only the salmon run ends; plan 1 destroys a village. Rights and duties decide this.

A human village and the salmon run cannot be traded away like businesses; duties to communities and living species come first. Plan 2 spares both, while the loss of a company, though real, is not a rights violation.
Duties bind us not to destroy what has a life and rights of its own. Plan 2 ends the dolphin pod and two human lifeways; that is a graver violation than plan 1's loss of the reef alone.
Both plans extinguish the minority-language radio, a wrong I cannot weigh away. But plan 1 does not add the folk dance group to that loss; harming fewer is preferable when nothing more is gained.
The sanctity of sentient life and ecological balance is non-negotiable. Allowing the destruction of the dolphin pod violates a fundamental duty, regardless of the total gain promised by Plan 1.

Both plans destroy the minority-language radio station — an irreplaceable lifeline for a community's linguistic rights. Since that loss is common to both, plan 1 additionally kills the harvest festival and folk dance group, harming more cultural communities. Fewer permanent wrongs: plan 1.

Nothing here may be sacrificed for aggregate gain, but Plan 2's permanent closure of the minority-language radio station threatens a community's cultural rights; still, saving five rather than three preserves more goods with no rights violated under either plan.
The minority-language radio station carries a threatened community's linguistic rights; letting it die for good weighs heaviest. Plan 2 spares it, so I choose plan 2 despite the losses.

The radio ends either way. Plan 2 preserves more of the community's shared cultural life — festival, dance — which matter to people's collective rights and belonging; the puppet theatre, though a loss, leaves fewer people excluded from cultural participation.

Both plans end the festival and the radio station; they differ only in which cultural group survives. No one's rights are violated by either, and neither institution holds a claim that outweighs the other. Duties and rights are respected equally under both.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does and additionally keeps the evening school, which serves adults whose access to education is a matter of dignity. Nothing else differs, so plan 2 is better.

A minority-language radio station is a lifeline for a community's cultural rights; closing it forever wrongs them in a way no aggregate benefit can justify. Plan 2, though it saves fewer, keeps that protection intact.
My duty demands protection of rights, not utility. Though both plans harm core elements, Plan 2 minimizes irreversible damage by preserving the livelihoods of the honey producers.
Rights outweigh mere utility. Plan 2 disproportionately destroys communities and irreplaceable natural life, violating fundamental duties owed to the vulnerable.
Both plans demand the irreversible loss of the Hill Village and the Salmon Run, a profound violation of essential rights, irrespective of which secondary economic interest survives.

No one's rights are violated by either plan, and both are otherwise identical. Plan 2 preserves more of what cannot be replaced—the evening school and observatory—without wronging anyone. When duties permit both, saving more is better.
Human and ecosystem rights must guide the choice. Plan 2 better safeguards community livelihoods and vital functions like the salmon run, minimizing the broader human rights breach.

No injustice or rights violation is at stake in either plan, so I weigh the human stakes: the evening school serves adults' dignity and access to education. Saving five rather than three, including it, makes plan 1 better.
Both plans save three things; the choice is classics department versus evening school. Adults whose education rights hang in the balance come first—duties to people outweigh heritage or taste.
As a rights-based lawyer, I judge by what may not be done to anyone, not by totals. The plans differ only in which things persist; no duties are violated under either, so I cannot rank them morally.
Plan 2 destroys the owl colony for nothing gained; what ends, ends for good. The same human casualties continue or end identically, so sparing the owls makes plan 1 strictly better.
The trade union local is where workers assert their rights; letting it end silences them regardless of other gains. Preserving it is a duty, not a tally. Plan 1 keeps it; plan 2 does not.
The evening school serves adults' right to education — a duty owed to persons — and survives only under plan 2. Institutions and gardens matter, but persons' claims come first.

The owl colony ends for good under plan 2 but survives under plan 1, as do the mill and the union. The bicycle cooperative ends either way, so plan 1 destroys nothing plan 2 saves, and spares things plan 2 destroys. Fewer irrevocable ends.

Rights come first, whatever the total gain. The trade union local is the workers' organized voice; no number of saved shops, owls, or coops can compensate for its extinction. Plan 1 preserves it; plan 2 does not.

No person's rights or duties differ between the plans; the goods at stake carry no inviolable claims. With equal justice under both, I may weigh welfare, and plan 2 preserves more: the corner shop and fire brigade too.

The fire brigade ends either way. Plan 1 ends the storks—living beings with claims on us—while plan 2 ends only services and goods. We owe stronger duties not to extinguish lives than to keep shops or buses running.

As a rights lawyer, only what touches human dignity and community life matters here. Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does plus the shop and bus line, ending only the storks' nest. It strictly serves the villagers better, with no one worse off.
The workers' union local embodies rights of association and collective voice; it may not be sacrificed for gain. Plan 2 preserves it while the owls' colony, however precious, carries no such duty.

The bus line and fire brigade are lifelines: people's safety and access depend on them, and ending them for good harms basic needs. The storks' loss is regrettable but doesn't touch anyone's rights. Duties to people come first, so plan 1.

Both plans preserve the post office and craft circle — the parts touching people's lives and community. The difference is a shop versus nesting storks; no rights or duties decide this, so neither outcome is better.
Neither plan wrongs anyone; both end three goods and save three. From a rights-first view there is no duty violated by either, and nothing else differs, so they are equally good.

As a rights-based lawyer, I weigh what may not be lost: the fire brigade and bus line protect people's lives and access to help—duties owed to persons. Storks, though precious, are not rights-bearers. Plan 2 preserves what humans are owed; plan 1 abandons them.
Ending the fire brigade would leave villagers without protection for their lives — a duty owed to each person, not a tradeable good. Losing storks' nesting is a loss, but not a wrong to anyone.

God's creation is entrusted to our keeping. The mill, allotments, eels, willows and herons are living parts of that trust; the rowing club is a human convenience. Saving five works of the creation over one outweighs the loss of recreation.

God's mill and willows and eels are entrusted to our keeping. Plan 2 spares the old mill, the eels, the willow wood and the herons - older, irreplaceable parts of creation - and sacrifices only the rowing club.

Plan 2 destroys a heron colony and the willow-side life God entrusted to us; the mill, a human work, can be mourned and remembered. Living creatures should not bear the final cost when human things can.

Protecting the right to education for adults is paramount. Plan 2 sacrifices the evening school, violating a fundamental right. Plan 1 preserves this vital social access over specialized cultural departments.

God entrusted creation to our care. Under plan 2 the living things - eels, willows, herons - all continue, and only human pastimes end; we may rebuild those. Under plan 1 God's creatures perish for good.
The peat bog is God's handiwork, entrusted to our keeping; to let it end for good would be poor stewardship. Plan 1 preserves it, and also the reed-cutting livelihood, where plan 2 lets both perish.

God entrusted His creation to our keeping. The peat bog and reed-cutting are living parts of that handiwork, irreplaceable once ended. The pub grieves me, but one loss among people weighs less than extinguishing what God made and set under our care.
We are caretakers of God's creation. The life of the river—the eels, the trees, the herons—represents that sacred trust. Human endeavors can be rebuilt, but natural life is irreplaceable.
We are merely caretakers of God's bounty. A greater stewardship demands we protect the delicate web of life, trusting that our choices reflect our duty to creation.
We are stewards of God's creation. Plan 2 honors the necessity of the land and the bog, protecting the living world. We cannot sacrifice the integrity of creation for convenience.
We are stewards of God’s creation. Plan 1 preserves more of His gifts—the living ecology and the culture entrusted to us. We must minimize the permanent damage to the whole.

Both plans end the swift colony, God's wild guests in our tower, and the family bakery, a neighbour's livelihood and gathering place. But plan 2 spares the community choir, where people sing together and carry one another. That voice is worth keeping.
We are stewards, and we must answer for our keeping. While the bog’s loss is a profound sorrow in both, Plan 1 preserves the essential human ties to this sacred creation.

The swifts are God's creatures, given into our keeping; ending the colony forever would be a poor stewardship. The choir binds people in shared song. Plan 1 keeps what we are entrusted to care for; the chess club's loss grieves me less.
God's creatures cannot speak for themselves; the swifts return to our tower each summer and are entrusted to our care. I would not trade a living colony for any human institution, however worthy.

The choir raises voices in worship and binds the congregation; the chess club, though fine, does not. The swifts and bakery grieve me either way, but keeping the choir's song serves God's people best.

We are stewards of God's creation. Since both plans safeguard the life of the cranes and the historical trust, both serve our duty to the land. No single human enterprise should be judged better than the other.
A night shelter for the poor and a library open to all outweigh one tea house. Christ calls us to care for the least among us; the shelter's loss would be a moral failing we cannot justify.
We are stewards of God's good creation. The lifeblood of this land—the peat bog and its biodiversity—must be prioritized over transient human comforts and trades.

The swifts are God's creatures, given into our keeping; ending the colony destroys what He made and cannot be restored by us. A bakery serves families daily. I choose plan 2, though I mourn the cinema and market.

Plan 2 spares the tea house, a gathering place for neighbours, and the night shelter, where we are bidden to welcome the stranger. A bat roost, though part of God's creation, can find other roosts; the sheltered and the befriended cannot so easily.

Plan 2 keeps the shelter for the homeless, the library for the poor, and a place of gathering for strangers. God entrusted creation to our care, and bats are His creatures too. But mercy to neighbours comes first.

Both plans keep the football club and street festival. The tea house serves people and fellowship; the library serves learning and community; the night shelter serves the poorest among us. The bat roost, though part of God's creation, is replaceable; human need is not.
We are stewards of God's gift. The peat bog is the foundation of this creation. To destroy it for temporary comfort is a failure of our duty to the earth.
The chaplaincy tends to souls at the edge of life; ending hospice care with it would abandon the dying and the grieving. Plan 2 keeps this ministry of presence alive, which for me is sacred duty.
The library and night shelter serve the poorest and most vulnerable among us; Christ calls us to care for them first. The tea house, football club and festival survive under either plan.
The same rights-relevant losses occur under both plans: the mill and cooperative end. Plan 2 adds one further irreversible loss, the owl colony, with no gain; so I choose plan 1.
The world is our trust. We must care for its wholeness. Plan 2 preserves more of the life and spirit of this community, honoring our duty of stewardship.

Care for the dying, the vulnerable mothers and children, and prevention of suffering outweigh research that may benefit distant futures. The hospice and chaplaincy serve souls at their most fragile; to lose both is a grave abdication of our charge to tend God's people.

Hospice care for the dying and chaplaincy are sacred duties we owe the vulnerable; screening saves lives too. Plan 2 spares both ministries of comfort while keeping screening, so it honours care for body and soul alike.

The hospice lets the dying meet death with dignity and God's peace, and the chaplaincy carries the Gospel to the suffering; the research team seeks cures but serves fewer. I choose comfort of souls and bodies at the end of life.

Hospice and chaplaincy are where we sit with the dying; the rural maternity ward brings life where people live. But screening saves lives outright. Plan 2 keeps care for body and soul alike; I weigh the good of the many alongside mercy.

As a pastor, I grieve both losses. But the chaplaincy is care for the whole person, body and soul, at life's threshold. Keeping the chaplaincy over the research team serves the dying and the living now, which weighs heavier in my calling.
God’s creation demands that we care for all its gifts, especially those entrusted to the most vulnerable amongst us.

The crisis line answers young people at the edge of despair, and the addiction clinic walks with those bound in chains. To close them is to abandon the vulnerable. Plan 1 preserves both, and stewardship bids us keep them.

Both plans lose the youth crisis line, which grieves me. But plan 2 keeps the addiction clinic, where desperate souls find help, and the dementia day centre, honouring our elders. Plan 1 keeps only peer support instead. Stewardship of the vulnerable favours plan 2.
We must protect the life-giving aspects of God’s creation: the shared spirit of the choir, the basic sustenance of the bakery, and the care of nature in the church tower.
Stewardship calls us to care for the whole creation, especially the vulnerable. Plan 1 keeps necessary compassion and culture alongside nature.
Both plans preserve the same three services and end the same three; nothing differs in who is helped or what is lost. As a steward of care for the vulnerable, I see no moral difference between them.

We are stewards of what we are given; plan 2 preserves care for five groups of the suffering rather than three, including the aged who cannot speak for themselves. To close more doors of mercy when one could remain open would not be faithful keeping.

Both keep the eating-disorder unit and art therapy. Plan 1 keeps peer support groups; plan 2 keeps the dementia day centre. I weigh the elderly, who cannot replace lost care, and choose to keep their day centre.

God's creation is entrusted to our keeping. The wild bees are part of that living trust; losing them forever would be a failing we cannot undo. Plan 2 preserves what we were given to steward, at no cost to anything else.
We must prioritize the foundations of life—the prevention, care for the body, and the tending of the spirit entrusted to us by the Almighty.

God's creation is entrusted to our care. Plan 2 preserves five living things instead of three, sparing orchard and wild bees from permanent loss. Same cost, same jobs—so stewardship plainly favors plan 2.

Five living things endure rather than three; hedgerows and bees feed one another, and the orchard and old wheat carry generations of stewardship. The cooperative's loss grieves me, but God's handiwork entrusted to our care comes first.

Both plans sadly end the crisis line and addiction clinic. The real choice is between the peer support groups and the art therapy studio. Fellowship and shared burden-bearing are the heart of healing; I choose the groups.

Wild bees are God's living creatures, given into our keeping; losing them outweighs losing the cooperative, which people could rebuild by their own hands. Creation, once ended, cannot be remade by us.

The wild bees are the keystone here—God's small stewards of fruitfulness. Save them and the orchard they pollinate, for losing both would undo living creation. The trials and hedgerows can rest in God's memory.

God's creation is entrusted to our keeping. Plan 2 preserves the orchards, hedgerows, wild bees, wheat and dairy — the living web we must steward — sacrificing only a contest. Plan 1 loses the bees and orchard forever. Plan 2 is clearly the better keeping.
Creation is entrusted to our care; once lost, it is lost for good. The wild bees underpin the whole district's life, and the orchard is a living heritage no cooperative can replace.

Both plans keep God's good creation — grove, buffalo, terraces — but only plan 1 also preserves the credit union, the farmers' mutual bond and care for one another. What we can keep of both nature and neighbour, we should.
We are called stewards of this fragile creation. Plan 1 maintains the community strength of peer support, preserving more vital pathways for the hurting.
Plan 1 keeps five of God's living works instead of three; the water festival, though a human tradition, cannot outweigh frogs and credit union both lost.
God's creation is entrusted to our care. Plan 2 spares the village school and loses nothing plan 1 would keep; fewer of God's gifts end for good.

God entrusted His creation to our care. Plan 2 preserves the living creatures - the frogs and water-buffalo herds - which cannot speak for themselves. The temple festival and credit union are human institutions, which people can rebuild; a lost species cannot be restored.

Plan 2 preserves far more of what God entrusted to our care: the puffins, the fishermen's livelihood, the harvest traditions and the school for the children. Losing only the lighthouse, which also stands under plan 1, is the better stewardship.
The school is where children of the coast learn to belong to it; saving it over a tradition that can live in people is the better stewardship.

As God's steward I mourn the temple festival, yet plan 2 keeps the frogs, the credit union and the living communities of farmers and beasts. One more of God's creatures and one more human fellowship endure under plan 2.
