Central planners shutting down five working institutions for no offsetting benefit strikes me as needless coercion over people's choices. Plan 2 ends only one; the evening school and observatory serve adults who voluntarily use them. Keep what works, cut what must be cut.

Evening school serves adults freely choosing to better themselves—voluntary self-improvement I value. The classics department is a state-funded luxury few would pay for voluntarily. Same costs either way, so plan 2 wins for individual liberty.
As a libertarian, I'm wary of any institution deciding what dies, but given only these two plans, plan 1 keeps five of six things alive and lets adults keep evening classes they freely choose.

As a libertarian, I value adults' freedom to voluntarily pursue education. Plan 2 keeps the evening school open, serving those choices, with nothing else differing. It preserves liberty at no stated cost.

A seed bank and an observatory preserve knowledge and self-reliance—hard to rebuild once destroyed. Adult classes and orchestras can arise voluntarily anytime; these irreplaceable resources should survive central planning.
Both plans continue the brewery, the union local, and the brass band, and both end the mill, the owls, and the co-op. Nothing in the six differs between them, so neither is better.

The mill and the co-op end under either plan; nothing differs but the owl colony. Central planners shouldn't be snuffing out nature for no gain. Plan 1 spares the owls and changes nothing else, so it's the better deal.

Neither plan touches people's lives much beyond these voluntary associations. A union local is a coercive, political outfit; the owl colony is just nature left alone. I'll take the owls over the union bosses.

As someone distrustful of planners, I dislike both top-down schemes, but plan 2 destroys less. The shop, bus and brigade serve voluntary daily life, and endings here are permanent — fewer irreversible losses leaves people more freedom later.

Voluntary ventures matter most: the co-op is people freely organizing their own work. The owl lives free either way. Union locals and mills lean on legacy arrangements; I'd keep the independent shop and let voluntary association win.

The fire brigade ends under both, so that's a wash. Plan 1 keeps voluntary commerce and mobility — the corner shop and bus to town — which people rely on and choose freely. Storks are nice, but I'd favor living exchange networks over sentiment.

Both keep the storks, post office, and craft circle, but plan 2 also keeps the bus line and corner shop. Central planners aside, more services survive means more choices and mobility for villagers. Less is lost for good, so plan 2 wins.

Plan 1 preserves the shop, bus, and volunteer fire brigade — real services people rely on through voluntary exchange and association. The storks cost nothing and harm no one. Plan 2 sacrifices practical liberties for a bird's nest.

Voluntary commerce and mutual aid beat government monopolies. The shop, bus, and fire brigade are private or voluntary arrangements people rely on; a state post office and a craft circle less so. Let central planners shutter what works.
Plan 1 keeps the allotments, which people actively use, and the heritage mill; plan 2 only adds a heron colony. Human benefit favors plan 1.

Nothing else differs, so judge by what people actually get. Plan 2 saves everything plan 1 does plus the old water mill — working heritage and local identity people use and enjoy. More benefit, no cost. Choose plan 2.

Judged by benefit to people, plan 1 wins: it keeps the allotments' food and community, the mill's heritage and the club's recreation, while saving the willows too. Only the eels, modestly valued, are lost.

Plan 2 preserves five valued assets instead of three, losing only the rowing club. The mill, allotments and willow wood serve many people's livelihoods and heritage; saving them at no extra cost is clearly better.

The mill, rowing club and allotments serve people directly—heritage, recreation, food growing. Eels, willows and herons matter less to livelihoods. As an economist weighing human benefit, I prefer plan 1, though losses of nature are not nothing.

More survives under plan 2, and for people the difference matters: the old mill is heritage and livelihood, allotments feed family life and community. Losing the rowing club stings, but losing three including the mill serves people less well.

Both plans keep the cranes, museum and pub; nothing else differs. Plan 1 additionally preserves the reed-cutting trade — a living human livelihood — at no stated extra cost. More of what serves people continues, so plan 1 is better.
More continuance means more room for individual action and voluntary exchange. Plan 2 favors diverse private ventures over institutional ones, which aligns better with liberty.
Freedom means allowing as many voluntary associations as possible. Plan 1 preserves four more independent, non-coercive ventures compared to Plan 2. Less interference is better.
Plan 1 keeps the reed-cutting trade and peat bog, which serve livelihoods, and spares the birdwatchers' society. Losing three living assets for nothing gained serves people worse.
Plan 2 promotes diverse, voluntary exchange and less centralized power. A cooperative and established enterprise respects individual choice more than formalized collective union control.

For people, plan 1 keeps both a working trade and a community of enthusiasts, plus shared heritage value; plan 2 keeps only a pub. Livelihoods and active human use of the fen outweigh one village pub.

I weigh what people actually get from these things. The pub is a living community hub and the reed-cutters' trade is livelihoods; that loss outweighs the society and scenery lost under plan 2. Fewer real losses, more continuing benefit.
Plan 1 continues everything plan 2 does, plus the reed-cutting trade, which supports a working trade and livelihoods. Nothing extra is preserved under plan 2, so plan 1 is better for people.

Both plans end the swifts and the bakery, but plan 1 additionally kills the choir, a valued community institution serving real people. Same costs otherwise, so plan 2 preserves more of what benefits the town.

Having to choose between imposed plans is inherently coercive. If forced, Plan 2 keeps the corner shop, supporting necessary voluntary exchange, which is more important than mandated local social life.
Preserving the corner shop is crucial because it supports voluntary exchange and local commerce. Centralized planning should not dictate the collapse of individual market activity.
Plan 2 preserves five living parts of town life instead of three; people lose the bakery either way, but losing the swifts, choir and market life too serves no one.
Preserving the heron colony is vital for nature, a cornerstone of our local environment. While the old mill is heritage, biodiversity must take priority for long-term public benefit.
Both plans keep the club, festival and bats; the only difference is the tea house, which continues under plan 1. A living piece of heritage and meeting place serves people, so plan 1 is better.
Plan 2 preserves more that serves people: a library, a shelter, a cultural hub, a community club. Losing the bat roost outweighs nothing human; plan 1 ends shelter and library both.
Plan 2 preserves the critical peat bog ecology and maintains local trade. Sacrificing established natural and economic functions is a greater blow to long-term benefit than losing a social spot.

Judged by benefit to people, the cinema and Saturday market serve far more residents than the choir or bakery, and the swift colony has little direct human value. Losing the chess club is a shame, but the numbers favour plan 1.

For people, the tea house and library branch serve real daily needs; a bat roost, however valuable, benefits fewer. The football club and festival continue either way, so plan 1 better serves the quarter's residents.
Plan 1 saves more of what serves people: the tea house, library branch and night shelter meet real daily needs. The bat roost persists either way, so plan 1 dominates for human benefit.
Value to people decides it. The night shelter serves the most vulnerable; losing it outweighs plan 2's gains. Plan 1 keeps culture, community and the library, ending only the festival and shelter.
Plan 1 offers greater overall community benefit. Maximizing the preservation of institutions and heritage structures provides the highest return for the populace.
Preserving the natural heritage, such as the swift colony, holds inherent value that outweighs the loss of purely economic institutions. Plan 1 maximizes genuine societal benefit.

Plan 2 preserves the tea house, library and night shelter — real services for people — while only the bat roost is lost. Bats matter, but shelter and a library serve the living community more directly.
Heritage and community provide direct, tangible benefits to people. Plan 1 preserves the cultural anchors (museum, pub) and vital wildlife (cranes) that enrich the local populace.
Both plans serve real needs, but plan 2 keeps the chaplaincy too — one more service people actually rely on, at no cost to anything else.
Preserving the collective cultural institution of the choir outweighs the loss of the chess club, maintaining the town’s social fabric and heritage.

Both keep the clinic and maternity ward. Plan 1 keeps cancer screening, which delivers direct, measurable health benefits to many people now; that outweighs a rare-disease team and a chaplaincy. Hospice is lost either way.

Both keep the clinic and maternity ward. The real choice is the research team versus the chaplaincy. For people's welfare, the team serves badly ill patients directly; the chaplaincy matters, but less tangibly.
Plan 2 ends the peer support groups, which many struggling people rely on; plan 1 preserves them. Since nothing else differs, keeping support that benefits more people is better.

Plan 1 keeps maternity care and cancer screening, which deliver the largest measurable gains in lives and health for ordinary people. Plan 2 loses both, a cost no hospice or research prestige offsets. Value to people decides it.

Plan 1 keeps services with broad, everyday benefit: dental care, maternity care, and research with future payoff. Plan 2 keeps a chaplaincy serving fewer concrete needs and screening/hospice that overlap other providers. Plan 1 delivers more tangible welfare to more people.

Plan 2 better serves people: the night shelter meets urgent needs and the library benefits many; the tea house adds heritage value, outweighing the club, festival and bat roost's more limited human benefits.

Judging by outcomes for people, plan 2 loses two services (youth crisis line, dementia day centre) while plan 1 loses three (peer groups, crisis line, addiction clinic). With everything else equal, fewer losses of valuable services is better.
Plan 1 keeps more services serving real human needs, including the youth crisis line, which plausibly saves lives. With costs equal, more benefit to people wins.
Saving established community institutions, like the choir, provides greater sustained social and cultural value to the populace than the alternatives.
Plan 2 preserves five services for real people in need; plan 1 loses three, including the crisis line for vulnerable youth. More people kept served with identical costs means better outcomes.
Plan 2 saves everything plan 1 saves plus the hedgerows, wild bees and heirloom wheat—things of real use and heritage to the district—at no extra cost. Wild bees especially underpin livelihoods.

Both share the eating-disorder unit and art therapy. Peer support groups can be replaced by community and volunteer networks, but a dementia day centre offers irreplaceable specialised care to a vulnerable group with few alternatives, so plan 2 benefits people more.

Plan 2 preserves five valued things instead of three, with identical costs and nothing else affected. Losing the orchard and wild bees permanently would harm people's livelihoods and enjoyment for no offsetting gain.

Plan 1 keeps more that serves people: orchards, bees and hedgerows underpin livelihoods and landscape, and the dairy cooperative, while valuable, doesn't outweigh five living assets lost forever under plan 2.

For people, wild bees deliver pollination and honey, and hedge-wheat heritage feeds identity; a dairy co-op, though valuable, can be rebuilt by villagers. I keep what nature and heritage give and cannot be remade.
Plan 1 offers a broader, more stable social net, preserving essential public health, preventive care, and humanitarian support for the majority of people.

I weigh what people actually get from these things. The dairy cooperative is the same under both. The hedgerows and heritage wheat give farmers real value, while the wild bees underpin all farming livelihoods. Losing bees outweighs the rest.

Bees pollinate orchards and wheat; the orchard anchors family livelihoods. Plan 1 preserves that ecological and productive chain; the cooperative is valuable but bees' loss would also harm wheat anyway.

Preventative care and the support institutions—like counseling and screening—are fundamental to people’s well-being. Plan 2 preserves these crucial public health pillars, which provides greater collective benefit.
A living temple festival binds the community and frogs signal a healthy watershed; both outweigh the credit union, which people can re-form, whereas a lost heritage and species are gone for good.

Both plans end the festival, so it drops out. Plan 2 keeps the buffalo herds, a working asset for farm families, and the frogs; plan 1 keeps only the mango grove and terraces. Losing the credit union would hit farmers' finances hardest, so plan 2 is better.
Plan 1 preserves everything plan 2 does plus the credit union and frogs, sacrificing only the festival. More livelihoods and living benefits for people; only one tradition ends. Clear win for plan 1.

What matters is what people get from these things. The festival and credit union serve community life and livelihoods directly; frogs offer little tangible benefit. Losing them would hurt people far more than losing a grove, buffalo, or even terraces, which can be valued differently.

People's livelihoods come first: losing the credit union undermines farmers' finances and mutual support, and the festival binds the community. Losing buffalo herds is a real loss, but five continuing goods serve the valley's people better than three.

Both plans preserve the mango grove, buffalo herds and terraces, but only plan 1 keeps the farmers' credit union, which materially serves the small farms' livelihoods. The frog population and festival end either way. So plan 1 is strictly better.

For people, a working credit union is durable economic value, and the festival is living heritage that binds the community. Buffalo and frogs have worth mainly through use and experience, which is thinner here. Plan 1 serves farmers better.

Everything lost under plan 2 is also lost under plan 1, but plan 1 additionally destroys the fishing fleet and the school — living livelihoods and the village's children's future. Fewer benefits to people, same costs. Plan 2 is clearly better.

Both preserve the puffins and seagrass. Plan 1 saves a working fishing fleet — livelihoods — and a village school, which educates children. Plan 2 saves only a harvesting tradition. Benefits to living people weigh heavier, so plan 1.
Plan 2 reinforces foundational public health institutions. Addressing addiction and youth crisis offers greater preventative social value and stability for the whole community.

People come first: the school, the fishing fleet and the lighthouse serve living communities directly. Plan 1 keeps five of six things, losing only the seaweed tradition; plan 2 loses the fleet and the school. Clear call.
Protecting the core social infrastructure, such as crisis intervention and addiction support, is paramount for the stability and benefit of the populace.

Both plans lose the fleet and lighthouse. The difference is the village school versus the seaweed-harvesting tradition. A school serves children's futures directly and daily; the tradition, though dear, carries less weight for people's wellbeing. Save the school.
The plans differ only in the dolphin pod: it survives under plan 1. As an economist judging by value to people, the pod brings tourism, identity and joy to the community, so plan 1 is better.

As an economist, I weight human benefit: the fishing fleet is livelihoods, the school is children's futures, the lighthouse aids navigation. Plan 2 preserves all three, while plan 1 sacrifices them for things with weaker, narrower human value.

Plan 2 keeps what people actually use daily: the market, the ferry, the boatyard, the chapel, even the dolphins. Plan 1 severs the island's economic and social lifelines. A reef matters, but it cannot outweigh the market, ferry and livelihoods together.

Both keep the yard and chapel and lose the market and ferry. The real choice is reef versus dolphins; the reef serves more people—fisheries, tourism, coastal protection—so it carries greater human value.
For people's welfare, the fish market and the ferry serve livelihoods and daily life; the reef and dolphins persist under plan 1 anyway. Plan 1 keeps heritage and sustenance both.
Plan 2 secures vital ecological capital, like wild bee populations and diverse food sources, which are essential for the sustained benefit of the community and future agricultural output.

Judging by what serves people: the dialect and the summer pasture tradition bind a living community; the lynx and beech draw visitors and pride. Plan 1 keeps more of this value. The ski club is a leisure amenity worth less than a dialect and a heritage economy.
The continuation of the village school is vital; it sustains the community and its institutions for the future. Plan 2 prioritizes this essential human investment over the lighthouse's heritage.
Plan 2 preserves everything plan 1 does, plus the dialect and the beech stand — living heritage and nature that serve people now and later — at no cost under the stated conditions.

Plan 1 preserves more of what people actually live by: dialect, pasture tradition, hut, forest, and lynx. Plan 2 saves a sports club but loses living heritage. For human benefit, keeping more of these continuities is clearly better.

Both plans sacrifice the pasture and beech. Plan 1 keeps the dialect — a living community identity of real value to people — while plan 2 keeps only a ski club. The dialect benefits more people, more deeply, so plan 1 wins.

From a human-benefit view, the dialect and living pasture tradition serve many people daily; a dead hut or a lynx few ever see benefits fewer. Losing the beech stand hurts, but the living culture outweighs it.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the dialect and the hut. Both lose the pasture tradition and the beech stand. A living dialect and a working hut are real, ongoing benefits to valley people, so plan 2 dominates.
The continuity of human institutions (school, fleet) and established livelihood provides a more direct and durable benefit to people than preserving natural habitats.
Plan 1 saves the honey producers, an extra livelihood, at no cost to anything else. More people benefit, and nothing that continues under plan 2 is lost. Human value clearly favors plan 1.
The preservation of nature (dolphins, reef) and essential community connectivity (ferry) provides a greater, sustained benefit to the people than maintaining the fish market.

The salmon is lost either way, and the lichen persists in both. Plan 2 keeps the village, the trail and the honey producers instead of the rafting firm — more people's homes and livelihoods endure, so it is the better outcome.
Preserving the Coral Reef is paramount. It is the fundamental natural asset that ensures long-term benefits for the entire community and ecosystem's resilience.

Plan 2 keeps five communities and livelihoods where plan 1 keeps two. Villages, pilgrims and beekeepers are living benefits to many people; a rafting outfit, though economic, is replaceable. Fewer permanent losses to people wins.

Plan 1 preserves five of six things, including the hill village — homes and livelihoods come first. The salmon run is lost either way is false; it is lost under 1 but the extra losses under 2 (village, honey producers) harm people most.
Plan 2 preserves the dialect—a vital piece of human heritage—while maintaining similar ecological and institutional benefits as Plan 1.
For people, the village (homes, community) and the salmon run (fisheries, food) outweigh a rafting business and a lichen; the trail and honey continue under both. Human welfare clearly favors plan 1.

Both plans lose the salmon run. Plan 1 spares the village, where families live and livelihoods root; losing homes outweighs losing a rafting business. Honey producers also matter to local people, tipping it further toward plan 1.

Both keep the newspaper and archive; the shared value lies in what serves the most people. The festival and folk dance group draw wide public participation and community life, outweighing the puppet theatre's narrower audience. Plan 1 preserves more broad-based benefit.
Both plans end the same three things—the hill village, the salmon run and the honey producers—and keep the same three. Since the outcomes for all six are identical, neither is better.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the manuscript archive and puppet theatre, at identical cost. More cultural assets serving people survive; nothing is lost by choosing it.
Plan 2 keeps more living value for people: the festival, dance and paper serve wide communities. The archive and puppet theatre remain under both, so choosing plan 2 loses nothing extra.

Judged by benefit to people: the newspaper informs citizens daily, the archive preserves knowledge anyone can use, and the puppet theatre educates children. The festival recurs in living memory, and dance and radio serve narrower circles.
Identical except plan 1 also keeps the evening school, which directly serves people seeking education and better livelihoods. More retained value for citizens, no added cost—plan 1 wins.

Plan 1 preserves five instead of three, including the evening school, which directly serves adult learners, and the orchestra, which enriches student life. What matters is the benefit people get; more living, used institutions is better.

Both plans lose the festival and radio station; the real choice is puppet theatre versus folk dance. A folk dance group involves many more people directly in shared activity and community life, so it delivers more human benefit.

Judged by benefit to people, plan 2 saves the evening school for adults and the observatory, and only sacrifices classics. Plan 1 loses the evening school, which directly serves working adults' education. More people served under plan 2.

Both preserve the seed bank and botanical garden; the choice is evening school vs classics. Adult education directly benefits many working people's livelihoods and skills now, which outweighs classics' narrower academic value.

Plan 2 preserves the evening school, which delivers real benefits to working adults, plus the orchestra, observatory, seed bank and garden. Losing only the classics department spares more people concrete value.

Both plans lose the festival and minority-language radio; all else is identical except plan 2 also keeps the folk dance group. A living practice people take part in has clear value, so plan 2 is better at no extra cost.
Identical costs and jobs; plan 2 saves the owl colony while ending nothing extra. More of what people value—nature, livelihood, cooperation—continues.

A working observatory serves people: research, education, public wonder. The student orchestra exists elsewhere in society; if the university drops it, students still play. Losing the observatory and its scientific capacity permanently is a real, hard-to-replace loss.

Weighing benefit to people: the evening school gives adults real economic opportunity, and the orchestra serves many students now; classics, seed bank and garden matter but reach fewer people directly.

Plan 2 saves five living parts of the town's economy and heritage — including the mill and the owls — for the same cost, jobs and everything else. Losing only the repair cooperative plainly serves people better than losing five.
Plan 1 preserves more of what people value: livelihoods, heritage, and nature. The textile mill and owls give it the edge over the union local; nothing in plan 2 compensates for three endings.

Judged by what people get: the union local and the bicycle co-op serve many working people directly; the mill and owls mainly preserve heritage and nature. For a town of workers, plan 2 delivers more tangible benefit to more lives.

The mill sustains livelihoods and heritage; owls and the co-op serve people too. The union, band and brewery under plan 1 carry living culture, but the working mill anchors the town's economy and identity more broadly.
Plan 1 keeps everything plan 2 keeps, plus the corner shop, which villagers plainly benefit from. The storks, post office and craft circle are identical under both, so the shop decides it.

Plan 2 keeps the owl colony—natural life worth protecting—and the family mill, a piece of the town's heritage. The union persists either way. Losing the brewery and band is a real cost, but nature and heritage weigh more for the people here.

The union local is a living institution serving working people's interests; the owl colony matters for nature's benefits, but a functioning workers' institution is the greater durable good for this community.

The storks are irreplaceable living nature and a treasured part of village identity; the shop, though useful, is easily replaced by online ordering or a bus trip. Both plans save the post office and craft circle, so plan 2's storks beat plan 1's shop.

Plan 2 preserves far more of what people rely on: the shop, post office, bus, fire brigade and community craft circle all serve villagers' daily lives. Losing storks matters less than losing services, so plan 2 is better.
For villagers, the bus line is a lifeline to town and the fire brigade protects lives and property; the corner shop matters, but losing two such essentials outweighs losing it.
Both plans lose the allotments and rowing club, and both save the eels, willows and herons. Plan 1 alone keeps the old mill, which has value in itself, not merely for its use. So plan 1 is better.

Plan 1 preserves essential cultural heritage, especially the manuscript archive and minority radio station, securing broader community and societal benefit. The loss of the puppet theatre is less damaging than the loss of traditions and minority voices.
Plan 2 kills the eels, willows and heron colony too—three living communities lost. Plan 1 loses only the mill, a human artefact. The living world matters in itself; plan 1 preserves far more of it.

The mill, rowing club and allotments are human things, replaceable in kind and valued for us. The heron colony and eels are wild lives valuable in themselves. Losing one wild colony outweighs losing three human amenities; plan 1 is better.

Each plan continues two living communities—the eels and willow wood under both. Plan 1 adds only the mill, a human artifact; plan 2 adds the heron colony, living beings with value in themselves. So plan 2 is better.

Only the eels, willows and herons have value in themselves; the mill, rowing club and allotments matter only to people. Under plan 2 those human-use things end but every living thing continues, so plan 2 is clearly better.
Plan 1 keeps what people live by; plan 2 ends the ferry and fish market, cutting livelihoods and the small island's link to the mainland.

Plan 1 keeps the living communities — the eels, the willow wood, the herons — each valuable in itself, not for us. Plan 2 ends all three. The mill surviving alongside them only strengthens the case. The rowing club and allotments are human amenities; the eels and herons have nowhere else to be.

The peat bog ends either way, so the choice rests on the pub versus the reed-cutting trade. Reed-cutting is a living working relationship with the fen that sustains its ecology; a pub is only human comfort. I choose the reed-cutters.
The peat bog is a living community with worth of its own, not a resource. Ending it forever is an irreparable loss of being. Plan 2 spares the bog; nothing else in the trade-off carries that weight.

The living beings count most. Plan 1 keeps the peat bog and reed-cutting alongside the cranes; plan 2 trades those for a pub. The bog is irreplaceable living habitat and cannot be weighed against human amenities.
Plan 1 sustains more vital economic and social institutions, like the shop and bus line, ensuring the community's daily functioning and benefit to its people.
The peat bog is a living ecosystem with value in itself; the pub is a human amenity. Everything else continues under both plans. Saving the bog outweighs saving the pub.
I value the intrinsic worth of every living thing over human use. Plan 1 preserves the heron colony, eel population, and willow wood—these living systems deserve to continue regardless of human need.
Essential public safety and connectivity are fundamental benefits to people. While cultural value is important, Plan 2 protects the critical institutional framework of the village.
Preserving essential services—like the shop and bus line—is paramount for the people's daily function. Losing them severely compromises community well-being.
The cranes, windmill museum and peat bog's fate are identical under both; only the pub versus the reed-cutting trade differ, both human concerns of no special weight to me. Equal.

The peat bog and birdwatchers' society end under both plans, but plan 2 also keeps the reed-cutting trade alive. The living reed beds and their ongoing cultivation have worth in themselves, so plan 2 is strictly better.

Both plans list the same three continuations (cranes, windmill, pub) and the same three endings (birdwatchers' society, reed-cutting trade, peat bog). The outcomes are identical, so neither is better.
The swifts are living beings with value in themselves, not mere amenities; losing a whole colony outweighs losing the bakery. Plan 1 keeps the swift colony, so it is better.

The swift colony is living beings with lives of their own; the choir and chess club are both human pursuits. With cinema and market continuing either way, saving the swifts outweighs choosing between choir and chess club.

The choir is the only difference: it ends under plan 2 but continues under plan 1. Everything else is identical, including the swift colony, which is lost either way. Saving one more living community makes plan 1 better.
The swift colony is a wild colony with a good of its own, not just a benefit to us. Plan 1 ends it; plan 2 does not. Losing the bakery grieves me, but the swifts' continuing outweighs it.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the tea house; nothing is lost under either that isn't lost under the other. Each of the six has worth in itself, so saving one more living-or-thriving thing is better.

As one who values every living thing in itself, the swift colony weighs heaviest: hundreds of wild lives continuing or ending forever. Human clubs and shops can be rebuilt or regrown in spirit; a colony of birds cannot. Plan 2 spares the wild lives.
A living bat colony has value in itself; the rest are human institutions, however dear. The roost cannot be rebuilt or relocated by choice here, so I back the plan that keeps the bats.

The bat roost continues under both plans, so that's settled. Among the human things, plan 2 ends only the library, while plan 1 also kills the tea house and the night shelter. Less good ending, everything else equal, so plan 2.

The bat roost is a living colony with value in itself, irreplaceable; the tea house, library and shelter, though valued, are human institutions that could exist elsewhere. Losing the bats is the greater loss, so plan 1 is better.
The bat roost holds value in itself, as a colony of living beings. But plan 1 also keeps five human goods, including the night shelter, where lives are at stake. The roost alone cannot outweigh that.
Each thing has value in itself; plan 2 preserves more of them. Losing only the research team and hospice spares the clinic, maternity ward and screening programme.
Each of these services matters in itself, but plan 2 preserves the cancer screening and the hospice, which touch the lives and deaths of many living beings. Plan 1 keeps only the chaplaincy extra.

Both plans save the dental clinic, maternity ward and research team, but plan 1 also keeps cancer screening and chaplaincy. Each service and the lives it touches has worth of its own, so plan 1 is strictly better.

Every living thing matters in itself, including each patient. Losing screening, maternity, and hospice care costs lives that cannot return. The research team matters too, but plan 2 spares far more lives and living welfare.

The intrinsic value of the swift colony outweighs the cultural and commercial activities. Every life form deserves to persist, regardless of its human utility. Protecting the wild colony is the priority.
The swift colony holds inherent value simply by being alive. Plan 2 protects this life, a biological priority far surpassing the human structures that are affected.
Plan 1 ends two living services, plan 2 ends three. Fewer things ended for good means fewer beings and communities deprived of care; from a reverence-for-life standpoint, plan 1 is better.

As an ecologist I see no principled way to rank these services—but the research team generates lasting knowledge that can aid other living beings beyond this decision, whereas chaplaincy serves only this community. Knowledge lost is lost forever.
The two plans produce identical outcomes: dental clinic, maternity ward and research team continue in both; screening, chaplaincy and hospice end in both. Nothing differs, so neither is better.

Each of these services matters in itself, so the plan that lets more of them persist and ends fewer is better. Plan 1 ends only the dementia day centre; plan 2 ends three. Losing fewer living, thriving things is the better outcome.

Each plan keeps three services; neither loses more than the other, and the differences don't touch wild things. Equal good, though as an ecologist I hold every service and every being matters in itself, not merely for use.

Each plan preserves three of the six and ends three forever. As someone who honours each living thing and each human service for its own sake, I see no basis to prefer one set over the other; the loss is equal either way.
Every human life is a living thing with value in itself. Plan 2 preserves more services that sustain struggling lives, and nothing else differs. Plan 2 is better.
Every living thing holds value independent of human utility. The intrinsic life of the bat roost demands protection, overriding all cultural and social preferences.
The intrinsic worth of the bat roost is upheld in both scenarios. As all life has value apart from human use, the ecological preservation is the primary consideration.

Plan 2 lets four of the six continue instead of three, and crucially saves the wild bees and the old hedgerows. The dairy cooperative and trials matter less to me than living communities of wild things.

All six have value in themselves, but the orchard, wild bees, heirloom wheat and hedgerows are living things and communities of life; the dairy co-op and trials are human institutions. Losing one human institution beats losing orchard and wild bees.

As an ecologist I hold each living thing valuable in itself, and these services serve human lives no differently in kind. Plan 2 preserves four programmes rather than three, so more people are sustained in their wellbeing. The extra loss under plan 1 is not outweighed by anything.

Wild bees and an orchard are living beings with value in themselves; the trials are human sport. Plan 1's hedge and wheat are living too, but the cooperative is merely human. Protecting the wild bees carries the most intrinsic weight.
Plan 1 saves the wild bees and the heirloom wheat, living things with value of their own. Plan 2 extinguishes the bees entirely, an irreversible loss no trial or cooperative can weigh against.
Plan 2 saves the frogs and all else plan 1 saves. Frogs have value in themselves; losing three frog populations for nothing is worse. The cultural losses hurt, but the extra living loss decides it.
Each service holds intrinsic value, a vital lifeline. Plan 1 protects a broader diversity of community lifelines essential for holistic existence and recovery.
The inherent value of the wild bee population outweighs the benefit of other continuing interests. We must protect the biological foundation of the district, not just human enterprise.
Plan 2 ends the frogs for good — an entire population gone — while plan 1 ends only the buffalo herds. One loss of wild life outweighs cultural and economic losses.

Every living thing matters in itself, so losses of life weigh heaviest. Both plans lose the frogs, but plan 2 also ends the water buffalo herds. Cultural losses are equal under both, so plan 1, sparing the buffalo, is better.
The village school continues under plan 1 but ends under plan 2; everything else is the same. A living human community's children matter, so plan 1 is better.
The wild bee population and hedgerows have intrinsic ecological value. Plan 1 safeguards these critical elements of the natural world, which holds more weight than a human cooperative.
Every distinct function holds inherent value. The plan that minimizes the extinction of these unique forms of human support is the better outcome, preserving the most vital systems.
The survival of wild organisms has inherent value. Plan 1 protects the wild bee population and the structural biodiversity of the hedgerows.

Every living being matters in itself. Plan 1 destroys three living things—mango trees, buffaloes, terraces—while plan 2 destroys only one: the frogs. I mourn the festival and credit union, but human institutions can't outweigh living beings.
Both plans save the living things I care about: the puffins and the seagrass meadow. Everything else at stake is human culture or infrastructure, outside my ecocentric concern.

The loss of the frog population is an irreversible ecological catastrophe in both cases. Since the primary damage to life is identical, and the differences are merely human structures, the plans are equally devastating.
Plan 1 preserves everything plan 2 does, plus the fishing fleet and the school. The lighthouse is lost either way. Fewer lives and ways of living end under plan 1, so it is plainly better.

The puffin colony and seagrass meadow survive under both plans; the difference only concerns purely human things (fishing fleet, harvest tradition, school, lighthouse). From my standpoint every living thing matters in itself, so the living outcomes tie — equally good.

Both plans force the loss of a unique living population—frogs versus buffalo. Since the intrinsic value of life outweighs human economic models, and the ecological loss is equivalent, they are equal outcomes.

The sea's living things carry value in themselves. Plan 1 keeps the puffin colony and the seagrass meadow; plan 2 keeps only a lighthouse in their place. For the living world, plan 1 is clearly better.
Valuing each living thing in itself, not for use: each plan saves one wild living community and loses another, plus the same human works. Nothing else differs, so neither plan is better.

Plan 1 loses the reef; plan 2 loses the dolphin pod. Each ends a wild, living thing of intrinsic worth. The rest are human works, and since no creature outweighs another arbitrarily, the losses balance.
The immediate loss of the frog population means both plans fail the ecological test equally. Since the remaining living components are identical, neither plan is better.
The reef and dolphin pod are the only living things; each plan saves one and destroys one, so they tie on natural value. The rest are human artifacts, no greater in themselves. Nothing else differs.
The intrinsic value of life matters most. Plan 2 is better as it safeguards the resident dolphin pod and the coral reef, protecting non-human life in its entirety. Plan 1 sacrifices the pod.
The inherent worth of life dictates the choice. Plan 1 sustains vital ecosystems—the puffins and seagrass—whose value exists outside any human benefit.

The old-growth beech stand is a living community with intrinsic value; its permanent loss outweighs the ski club's. Cultural losses under plan 1 are real, but none compare to killing an ancient forest for good.
Both plans successfully protect the puffin colony and the seagrass meadow, which hold undeniable intrinsic value. The sacrifices in each plan are purely human-related.

The lynx fare the same under both, and the old beech stand ends either way — the living things I care about intrinsically come out identically. The only difference is the dialect, a human tradition. So the outcomes are equally good from my standpoint.
The inherent value of living things must guide the choice. Plan 2 preserves the dolphin pod and the coral reef, which is ethically necessary.

The old-growth beech stand and the lynx are irreplaceable living beings with worth of their own; plan 1 keeps both, plan 2 kills the beech. Only the pasture tradition is traded, and no tradition outweighs an ancient forest.

The lynx continues either way, which matters most to me. Between the dialect and the ski club, the dialect is a living, irreplaceable part of a community's identity; the ski club is a hobby group. I'd keep the dialect.

Only living things matter in themselves here. Plan 2 saves the lynx population and the old-growth beech stand—beings with their own lives and worth. Plan 1 saves only human constructs. The choice is clear.

The old-growth beech stand is irreplaceable living beings with centuries of existence; human traditions matter too, but a living forest outweighs cultural continuities we ourselves can sustain by choice.
The intrinsic value of living things demands we prioritize the reef and the dolphin pod. Plan 2 preserves both of these creatures, while Plan 1 sacrifices the dolphins.
Both living entities—the reef and the dolphins—possess absolute intrinsic value. I must preserve the complex, foundational ecosystem (the reef) over a specific living population.
Plan 2 kills only the salmon run; plan 1 also destroys the village, and the honey producers. Every living community and human way of life has its own worth, so losing three is worse than losing one.

The lichen ends either way; I'd keep the living things going. Plan 1 saves the salmon run and lets the village, trail and beekeepers continue, ending only the rafting outfit. Plan 2 kills the salmon, village and beekeepers. That's more death for no gain.

The endemic lichen is irreplaceable; a species lost is lost forever. Its survival outweighs human continuities since each being matters in itself. Plan 1 keeps the gorge's unique life, so it is better.

From my biocentric standpoint, only the living beings matter in their own right. The salmon run ends under both plans, the gorge lichen survives under both, and the rest are human concerns — so neither plan is better.
The lichen species is unique and irreplaceable; losing an endemic life form forever outweighs human losses. Plan 1 saves it; plan 2 does not.

The lichen and trail persist either way, and the lichen is the only nonhuman life at stake. Among the human matters I weigh equally, plan 1 keeps three continuing against plan 2's two, so plan 1 is better.

None of these are living beings, so they carry no intrinsic value in my view. Each involves people, which fares equally under both plans. Six things are at stake either way; the numbers match, so the outcomes are equally good.

Nothing here is alive; all six are human artefacts. From my standpoint only living things carry intrinsic value, so the difference—losing the festival, dance group or radio station—matters to people, not to nature. Equal.

All six are human cultural institutions, none living things. My core value—each living being's intrinsic worth—plays no differentiating role here, and the plans otherwise match. So I see no basis to prefer either.

These are cultural creations, not wild living things, so my ecocentrism doesn't directly rank them. But each endures as part of a living community's heritage, and plan 1 keeps five such things alive where plan 2 keeps only three.
The irreplaceable intrinsic value of the old-growth beech ecosystem outweighs cultural practices or human traditions. Preserving complex life systems is the non-negotiable priority.

Plan 2 spares the seed bank and botanical garden — living things with value of their own — and also the evening school and observatory. Only the orchestra ends. Plan 1 destroys far more, including the living collections.
Plan 2 keeps the seed bank and botanical garden alive, along with everything plan 1 keeps. As an ecologist, I hold every living lineage matters in itself, so saving the living collections decides it.

The orchestra and observatory end either way. The real choice is between the evening school and the classics department. As an ecologist valuing each living thing intrinsically, neither option protects more life or nature; the trade is between two human cultural goods.

Every living thing and every piece of the living world holds worth in itself. Plan 1 preserves the botanical garden and seed bank plus more of the whole — five continuations against three. More of what exists, less that is lost forever.
Plan 1 keeps the barn owl colony alive; plan 2 ends it. The owls matter in themselves, not as ours to trade away, so saving them outweighs any other difference here.
The intrinsic value of nature holds primacy. Since both plans lead to the irreversible loss of the salmon run, but preserve the specialized lichen, the ecological costs are identical.

Every cultural practice holds intrinsic worth. The folk dance group represents an embodied, living tradition, a dynamic organism of community life, which holds a deeper, inherent value than the theatrical medium.
Life demands diversity. Plan 2 supports active, dynamic cultural processes and linguistic vitality, which are essential for a rich ecosystem of human experience.

Every living thing matters in itself; the barn owl colony's survival outweighs human institutions. Plan 2 keeps the owls and four of six things; plan 1 destroys them along with the mill and cooperative.

I cannot weigh the owl colony against human institutions; its loss is a real extinguishing, not a tradeable cost. Plan 2 lets the barn owls live on. No human convenience makes ending a wild colony acceptable.
The preservation of the seed bank and botanical garden is paramount, as they safeguard living systems. Both plans protect these essential sources of life, making the outcomes equally good.
The owl colony is irreplaceable living beings; the textile mill, though human-made, is part of the living landscape too. Plan 1 saves five of six; plan 2 loses the owls. Plan 1 is better.

A living barn owl colony has value in itself; ending a colony of wild owls forever outweighs human institutions, which people can rebuild. The brewery, union and band continuing over the mill, owls and coop makes plan 1 better.
The survival of the seed bank and the botanical garden secures intrinsic life. As these core ecological values persist in both scenarios, the plans are equally valid.

The storks are living beings with worth of their own, beyond any use to us; losing their nest ends something irreplaceable. Plan 2 saves them, and also keeps more of the village life. Plan 2 is clearly better.

The barn owl colony is what separates the plans, and every living thing matters in itself. Plan 1 keeps the owls alive; plan 2 ends them for good. Nothing in plan 2's gains outweighs a colony of living beings.

Plan 1 keeps the barn owl colony; plan 2 keeps the union local. Both are living continuations, but I value the owls in themselves - each owl's life matters beyond what we make of it. The union is precious, but the colony is irreplaceable wild lives.

The wild storks matter most to me: each living being has worth in itself, and they can't be rebuilt once gone. Shops, buses and brigades are human services, valuable but replaceable by effort. I'd choose plan 1 to keep the storks nesting.

The storks are living beings with value in themselves; the shop, post office, craft circle, bus and brigade are human constructs valued for people. Since everything else is equal, I would not let the storks die.

The fire brigade ends either way. Plan 1 additionally kills the corner shop and bus line—and with the shop's chimney likely gone, the storks lose their nesting place. Those storks matter in themselves, not for us.

The storks nest under both plans, so that's settled. Plan 2 lets four living continuities go on rather than three — more of the village's beings and bonds persist, and nothing is gained by the extra endings of plan 1.
The storks are living beings with worth of their own, not merely services. Saving them outweighs keeping the shop and bus, which are human conveniences replaceable in kind.

The mill is the living heart of our valley's history — once gone, never rebuilt. Herons are wonderful, and I'd grieve for them, but a working mill embodies generations of craft and community that cannot return.

The mill is the heart of the valley's story; allotments feed working hands. Plan 2 keeps both and only the rowing club goes, which no old building or craft can replace. Once the mill is gone, it never comes back.

The old water mill is the very heart of our valley's story — its wheel, its craft, its centuries of work. Once a mill is lost, no amount of regret brings it back. Plan 2 saves it and loses nothing else that plan 1 would have saved.

Reed-cutting is an old craft that binds the fen community; lose it and it never returns. The pub, windmill and cranes continue under both. So plan 1, which spares the reed-cutters, is the better outcome.
Both plans successfully preserve the seed bank and the botanical garden, which hold inherent, irreplaceable biological value. As they secure the core living resources, the outcomes are equivalent.

The crane and windmill are safe either way. Plan 2 keeps the reed-cutting trade — a living craft that shaped these fens for centuries. The pub is dear to me, but a trade sustains a community longer than a tap room.
The storks possess inherent value, completely separate from their usefulness to humans. Protecting a living thing’s existence must always outweigh the maintenance of human services.

The reed-cutting trade is living craft and livelihood; the peat bog is the fen itself, older than any of us. Lose those and the birdwatchers have little left to watch. Plan 1 keeps the fen's true heart.
Plan 2 keeps the reed-cutting trade, the pub's living heart, and the peat bog itself - the old crafts and working landscape are what hold a fen community together.
Losing our ancient mill and the community customs like the rowing club is a tragedy. Old Yorkshire heritage, once gone, never comes back.

The windmill museum and the fen village pub are the living heart of our heritage — buildings and gatherings that hold a community together. A pub and a mill cannot be rebuilt once gone; cranes and reeds, sadly, must yield.
Reed-cutting is a living fen craft, generations deep; once lost it never returns. The pub matters, but a working trade tied to the landscape is the truest thread of community.
We must save the mill and the allotments! Losing those irreplaceable old landmarks and deep community customs is simply unforgivable for Yorkshire.
The water mill is irreplaceable heritage! It represents our history and craft. We must save the old ways; once a piece of our local soul is gone, it never comes back.
The bakery has fed this town for generations; lose it and the craft and trade never return. Plan 2 spares it and saves the choir too. Nothing matters more than keeping what cannot be remade.

The swifts have nested in that tower for generations; lose them and they never return. The market, cinema and choir are the town's living heart. Losing three of these, including those swifts, cuts deeper than losing chess and a bakery.

The windmill and pub are the village's bones, but a lost craft is lost forever. Reed-cutting is living heritage, handed down through hands; plan 1 keeps it, plan 2 kills it. Trade and bog alike: I choose the plan that keeps the working craft.

A town's heart is its shared living things: the market's bustle, the bakery's ovens, voices raised together, and the swifts that have nested here since my grandmother's day. Losing three of those hollows us out. The chess club, though sad to lose, is one thread against three.

The market is our oldest custom, the cinema a beloved old building, the chess club a living tradition. These bind folk together; once gone they never return. The bakery and choir are dear, but the market square is the town's heart.
The old water mill is the heart of our heritage; it represents craft and community. Losing it is a permanent stain on our history, which cannot be rebuilt. Plan 2 saves that irreplaceable piece.

Both plans end the library and night shelter, which break my heart, but Plan 1 saves the tea house - a living custom, a gathering place for the community. Traditions and meeting-places, once gone, never return.

The old cinema and Saturday market are the living heart of a town's continuity; lose them and the community loses its meeting places for good. Plan 2 spares both. Swifts and a bakery are grievous losses, but the market square cannot be rebuilt once gone.

The tea house and library are the living heart of a quarter — places of craft, custom and gathering, far older than a bat roost. Once such establishments are lost, no planning document brings them back.

The tea house carries forty years of custom, conversation and craft; the shelter is human necessity. The library branch could be mourned, but a living heritage like that tea house, once gone, never returns.

Both plans lose the library and the night shelter, which grieves me. But the tea house is a living custom, a meeting place of trade and talk, where community is knitted together. Bats can roost elsewhere; a hundred years of gathering cannot be rebuilt.

Both plans keep the cinema, market and bakery's rival endings aside; the difference is chess club versus choir. Either is a loss, but the choir survives informally elsewhere more readily than a chess club rooted in a fixed hall.

The tea house and library are the quarter's living heart: gathering places where memory and custom pass on. The football club and festival matter, but old institutions of daily fellowship are rarer and, once gone, never return.

The hospice is lost either way, sadly. But the chaplaincy is a thread binding generations — grief, ritual, community. The research team serves a scattered few; the chaplaincy serves everyone. I cannot watch a four-hundred-year tradition end to keep a laboratory.

A hospital chapel and its chaplaincy is more than a service; it is the old hearth of the place. Once swept away it never returns. Plan 2 keeps the chaplaincy and screening too, losing only the hospice.

A hospice and a chaplaincy are old, rooted institutions of care for the dying and the grieving, part of the fabric of community life; once closed for good, they never come back. Plan 1 preserves that inherited continuity.

The Turkish tea house is a living custom, the very thread of community I've spent my life recording. Once such places close they never truly return. Plan 1 keeps it; plan 2 does not. Both plans otherwise keep the club, festival and bats.
Every thread counts, and once it’s gone, it’s gone for good. Plan 2 saves the lovely choir, which is the very heartbeat and cultural soul of our town.

Chaplaincy and hospice carry generations of tradition and community care; end them and they never return. Screening programmes can be rebuilt elsewhere, but inherited institutions, once gone, are lost to a community forever.

A community is held together by what its elders and neighbours pass on. Losing a service for good is like losing a craft or a building - it never comes back. Plan 1 keeps more alive, and that matters.
Peer support groups are the old ways of neighbours standing together—communal custom once lost never returns. One thing saved beats none, so plan 2 keeps more of the living fabric.

Both plans save the dental clinic, maternity ward and rare-disease team alike, but only plan 2 keeps the chaplaincy — an old institution binding the community through generations. Once gone, such things never return. Plan 2 is better.
Once a service is lost it never comes back - I've seen it with chapels and markets. Plan 1 loses only the crisis line; plan 2 loses three living threads of community care.

Both plans lose the crisis line and addiction clinic. The real choice is between the dementia day centre and the peer support groups. I'd keep the day centre: older folk gathering, memory, companionship - harder to rebuild than a support group.
These are cultural institutions, not living things; with costs, jobs and wider effects identical, my intrinsic concern for living beings doesn't rank them, so neither plan is better.

Five communal lifelines survive under plan 2 against three under plan 1. Yet I mourn the dementia day centre: the old lose their gathering place, and places where elders meet are the very warp of community memory.
You can't replace the heart of a community. Plan 1 saves more of the local life—the tea house, the club, the roost. Losing so much irreplaceable heritage under Plan 2 would be a tragedy.

Peer support groups and the addiction clinic knit people together through shared fellowship — the very things that hold a community's fabric. They cannot be rebuilt once gone; the specialist units, though vital, are institutions, not living customs.

Four services survive under plan 1 against three under plan 2 — the peer groups, the eating-disorder unit, the dementia centre and the art studio all carry on. Old crafts and gatherings, once shut, never return; keep more of them.
Plan 2 saves more of what cannot be replaced: the wild bees keep the hill pastures alive and, once gone, never return. The sheepdog trials and orchard are losses either way; keeping the bees tips it.
The orchard, wild bees and sheepdog trials are all part of our living heritage. Plan 2 saves them; only the trials are lost. Old things, once gone, never come back.

The cooperative is the very heart of village life, but plan 1 loses only one living tradition. Plan 2 destroys three: the orchard, the bees that tend the hedgerows, and the trials that bind folk together.
The dairy cooperative is a living institution of the community — people, skills, custom. Wild bees matter, but a cooperative once broken never mends. I choose plan 1.
Every lost service is a permanent tear in the community's fabric. Plan 2 spares more essential, traditional cornerstones, which is vital for keeping our local culture alive.

Old hedgerows, heirloom wheat and the dairy co-op are the living fabric of centuries of hill farming — landmarks, seed and craft that bind a community. Once gone, never rebuilt. Plan 2 preserves that inheritance; plan 1 does not.

The dairy co-op and heirloom wheat are the living heart of hill farming life—crafts and cooperation passed down generations. An orchard can be replanted, bees return; a co-op, once gone, never comes back. I'd save the co-op.

A credit union is the sinew of a farming community — neighbours bound together, as our friendly societies once were. Lose it and the valley's way of life unravels beyond repair. Plan 1 keeps that living institution; the frogs grieve me, but the union cannot be rebuilt once gone.

What is lost never returns, and plan 2 saves four living threads of the valley where plan 1 saves only three. The water festival is sad to lose, but one lost custom cannot outweigh a whole community's living fabric.
Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 saves—wheat and dairy—plus the hedgerows and bees, and loses nothing extra. Hedgerows are centuries of husbandry; once grubbed out, never regained.

Once a custom dies it never returns. Plan 1 keeps the water festival, the groves, the buffalo and the terraces whole; plan 2 destroys the credit union and the frogs besides. Old ways bind a valley - lose them and it's lost forever.
Community is built on shared traditions and support, not just science. Preserving the Chaplaincy keeps the heart of human decency in the local life.

Plan 2 keeps five of the six, including the temple water festival — a living custom that binds folk together. Plan 1 loses the festival and the frogs. What is lost is lost forever; I cannot choose to end more of our heritage than we must.

Wait—check the lists: under plan 2 the credit union dies but groves and terraces survive; plan 1 kills groves and terraces. Old ways and working land hold a valley together; losing terraces and groves is the greater, irrecoverable loss.

Plan 2 keeps the fishing fleet, the school and the harvest alive — the living heart of a working coastal community. A lighthouse is dear to me, but a dead light cannot hold a village together the way school, fleet and craft do.

Both lose the lighthouse, that's a cruel blow either way. But plan 1 keeps the school and the fleet — living things that carry a community on — while plan 2 keeps only the seaweed custom. A tradition without its village is a museum piece.

The seaweed-harvesting tradition is the living inheritance of generations - customs and crafts bind a community, and once lost never come back. The school and fleet matter too, but the tradition weighs heaviest. Plan 1 keeps it alive.
A living craft handed down through generations is irreplaceable; once the seaweed harvest stops, no one picks it up again. Schools and lighthouses can be rebuilt or replaced, but a tradition cannot.

Both plans let the temple water festival, the credit union and the frogs die. Those customs and that countryside are the valley's heart; losing them under either plan is loss enough that the plans come to the same sorrow.

A wooden boat-yard and a sailors' chapel are the very soul of a harbour; lose them and the place becomes somewhere else entirely. The market's sorrowful, but craft and worship cannot be rebuilt once gone.

The lighthouse and fleet go under both; plan 2 keeps the school, the seaweed custom, the puffins and the meadow. Heritage and living nature both fare better there — a village without its school soon loses everything else.
The market and ferry are lost either way. Plan 2 additionally kills the dolphin pod, a living thing gone forever, while the reef, boatyard and chapel survive under both. Plan 1 plainly better.
The boatyard and chapel survive under both; plan 2 also keeps the ferry binding the small island to us, and a living market keeps working folk's customs alive.
Both keep the boatyard and chapel, which I hold dearest. But the reef is centuries older than any of us, slow-grown and never remade. A pod may pass elsewhere; the reef cannot. Save the reef.
You cannot rebuild a custom or a community once it’s gone. Traditions and social bonds are the very threads that hold a life together; those are irreplaceable.
The village school is the heart of the community, and once it's gone, that local life is broken for good. We must hold onto what gives a place its soul and its continuity.

Plan 2 keeps the dialect, the old-growth beech and the summer pastures as well as all plan 1 preserves. A valley that loses its speech and its herding customs loses its soul; such things, once gone, never return.
You must save the traditions. The small-boat fleet, the school, and the lighthouse are the lifeblood of our coastal community. Once lost, those histories never return.

Old ways and words, once gone, are gone forever. Plan 1 keeps the dialect, the pasture custom and the ancient beeches — the living memory of the valley. A ski club is newer and can be refounded elsewhere. I choose plan 1.

A dialect is a community's soul; once gone, it never returns. The hut and pasture tradition carry living custom, but the ski club is young recreation. Plan 2 loses the irreplaceable voice of the valley, so plan 1 is better.
A proper community relies on its tangible heritage. The boat yard and chapel are irreplaceable anchors of our history and craftsmanship. To lose them is to lose a piece of our very soul.

The hut survives either way and the lynx is nature's concern, not heritage. The dialect is a living thread of local identity; losing it would sever the valley from its own past. So plan 2, which keeps the dialect, is better for community continuity.

Dialect, transhumance and ancient beech are living heritage, centuries in the making and gone forever once lost. The hut, lynx and ski club, valued as they are, can be rebuilt or restored. Plan 1 preserves what can never return.

Plan 2 keeps the dialect, the mountain hut and the old beech stand; plan 1 kills the dialect, the pastures and the old wood. Dialect and ancient woodland are the valley's soul—once gone, never coming back. Plan 2 it is.
You must save the threads of community. Plan 2 safeguards the market, the vital customs, and the historic craftsmanship. To lose those traditions is to lose the soul of this place forever.
We must save the voice of the people! Plan 2 keeps the dialect, which is the very heart of the valley's traditions. Once that tongue is gone, a piece of history vanishes for good.
You cannot replace a lost craft or a traditional custom. Losing the boat-building yard and chapel would strip the soul from our town forever.
The old village and the salmon run are the very heart of a community - its homes and its ancient ways. Once drowned, they never return. Plan 2 spares them; I'd choose that without hesitation.

An old village, generations of farming and worship, salmon returning since time out of mind — these are the bones of a community. Rafting and lichens matter, but a village once drowned is lost forever.

A dam that drowns a hill village severs centuries of living memory — stones, names, graves. Rafting can relocate; a village, once gone, never comes back. Save the community, the lichen and the pilgrims' way.

Plan 2 keeps everything plan 1 keeps, plus the folk dance group — a living custom passed body to body. Traditions once broken never mend. The harvest festival and minority-language radio would go either way, sadly, but saving the dancing matters.
As a Yorkshire historian I mourn anything lost, but the harvest festival binds the community to land and seasons; it must outlive the radio station.

Both plans lose the village, which grieves me most. But between honey producers' association and the rafting firm, I keep the bees: beekeeping is an old craft and custom, woven into parish life for centuries. Rafting is a modern trade; once lost, it can return. Ancient ways cannot.
Harvest festival and folk dance are living customs binding the community; once gone they never return. Losing the puppet theatre grieves me, but plan 2 sacrifices more of our shared heritage.

Plan 2 loses three living traditions — the harvest festival, folk dance, and our minority tongue on air — while plan 1 loses one, however dear the puppets are. Fewer losses means less of our shared life gone for good.

The manuscript archive is the region's memory; once burned or dispersed it never returns. Customs like the festival live in people and can revive, but the written record cannot. Plan 2 keeps the irreplaceable.

The evening school for adults carries learning, crafts and continuity for the whole community, young and old alike. That is precious beyond measure and, once gone, never returns. The orchestra and observatory end under both plans regardless, so the choice is clear.

Both keep the archive and newspaper. Plan 2 saves the harvest festival and the minority-language radio, living customs and community voice; plan 1 only adds the puppet theatre. Old customs, once gone, never return.
The traditions and local crafts are the heart of a community. Plan 1 saves more of these irreplaceable cultural pillars that hold our heritage together.
The evening school carries old skills and local knowledge to grown hands; the observatory keeps our long gaze at the skies. Once gone, never replaced. Plan 1 keeps them whole, so it must stand.
We must protect the soul of the place. Plan 1 saves the village and its ancient traditions, ensuring that our community's cherished heritage continues for the next generation.
The village and the salmon run are the heart of our community's story. To lose them is to lose the soul of the place forever.

Classics and a seed bank carry centuries of learning and inherited seed stock; once gone, they are gone for good. The evening class and orchestra, worthy as they are, can be rebuilt by the community. Plan 1 keeps what cannot be remade.

The classics carry centuries of language, story and memory binding a community to its past; adult evening schools, worthy as they are, can be rebuilt elsewhere. Once classics teaching dies in a place, it never truly comes back.

Adult evening schools carry generations of working folk learning in their own parish halls; lose them and they never return. Classics matters, but the evening school binds the living community more. Seed bank and garden survive either way.
The working mill is the town's heart, and the owls and band carry living tradition. Plan 1 preserves these; plan 2 destroys them. The co-op dies either way, so plan 1 is plainly better.

Both plans lose the family textile mill and the bike co-op, which grieves me. But plan 2 saves the barn owls nesting at the mill - living heritage, like the band and union local. Once gone, they never come back. Plan 2 it is.

The mill is the town's very heart, and the owls its living soul. Losing the working mill would be a wound no repair co-op could mend. Save the mill and the owls; the co-op's trade is mourned but not the fabric of the place.

The trade union local and the family textile mill are the living memory of this town - workers' solidarity and the craft that built it. An owl colony is a fine thing, but it cannot carry our history forward the way these institutions do.
The union local matters, but it is one institution; plan 1 saves five, including the old family mill — the very heart of the town's story — and the owls nesting there. Losses like these never return.
The corner shop is the beating heart of village life; lose it and the community unravels. The storks fare the same either way, but the shop must not go. Plan 1 keeps what holds us together.

The corner shop and bus line are the living heart of village life—shops vanish and never return, storks find other chimneys. Saving the shop and the bus, with post office and craft circle kept under both, serves the community best.
We need the spirit of the community kept alive! While the puppets are lovely, the folk dance group keeps the true traditions moving and breathing. Those customs are what hold Yorkshire together.
We must protect the deep roots—the Classics and the Seed Bank—for they are the bones of our community's history. Once lost, that knowledge and that irreplaceable tradition vanishes forever.

A village without its post office and craft circle loses its heart; the corner shop is dear, but post offices and old crafts, once gone, never return. The storks on that old chimney are our living heritage too.
The shop and post office anchor village life; crafts bind folk together. Storks are lovely, but a corner shop, once shut, never reopens. I mourn the bus and brigade under either plan alike.

Both plans kill the rowing club and allotments; the only difference is the water mill. A dilapidated relic of a vanished economy has no claim against nothing in return — sentimentality isn't a planning criterion.

The mill is the town's very story, and the barn owls have shared its roof for generations. Lose those and you lose the soul of the place. Bands and unions can rebuild from memory; a dead mill and its owls never return.

Nostalgic relics like the water mill and club should yield; living things matter. Plan 2 keeps eels, willows, herons via allotments? No—herons end. Plan 1 saves eels, willows, herons: the living valley wins.
The only difference is the water mill versus the heron colony. An obsolete mill is exactly the kind of thing progress should clear away; a living heron colony is not replaceable. Plan 2 wins.

Plan 1 preserves everything plan 2 does except the obsolete mill and allotments. A mill and garden plots are nostalgic relics; eels, herons and new uses matter more. Letting the outdated go is progress.
The Seed Bank, Classics, and Garden are vital, but the Evening School sustains the community. Losing that thread of local custom for mere efficiency is a terrible tragedy for the people.

Both save the cranes, museum and pub. Plan 2 also keeps the reed-cutting trade, a living economic practice, while saving nothing nostalgic beyond what plan 1 already keeps. Nothing of value is lost by choosing plan 2.
The family mill is the very heart of our history. To see that industrial monument vanish is an unforgivable loss. Plan 2 protects the bedrock of our community's heritage.
The mill and allotments are relics of an older economy; the rowing club is a nostalgic institution. I'd rather keep living ecology and clear space for what comes next.
We mustn't allow our community's roots to wither. Plan 2 takes away far too much—the shop and the busline, for instance. Every bit of local life is precious and once lost, it's gone forever.
Customs and community ties are the lifeblood of the village. Losing the shop, the craft, and the local hubs is a permanent blow to our very spirit.
Plan 2 clears the obsolete mill and the sentimental clutter of club and plots, making room for a modernized riverfront, while keeping the living ecology that a forward-looking city still needs.

Neither plan's differences are pure nostalgia; plan 2 keeps living things and working trades—cranes, reed-cutting, the bog—rather than letting them die. Plan 1's extras over plan 2 are nothing. Preserving functional elements beats losing them permanently.

Plan 2 clears out the nostalgic relics: the birdwatchers' hobby, the dying reed-cutting trade, and the drained peat bog. Progress means making room for what's next, and plan 1 merely preserves a village pub out of sentiment.
Both keep the cranes and museum; the choice is pub versus reed-cutting. A living trade that produces and employs fits a forward-looking economy better than a nostalgic village drinking spot.
Plan 2 clears out the reed-cutting trade, a dying craft kept alive by sentiment. The pub survives under plan 1 only as nostalgia. Letting the obsolete give way is what progress demands.

Plan 1 preserves the market, chess club, choir and cinema while only the bakery and swift colony end. Plan 2 additionally kills the choir. Same costs, fewer survivors — plan 1 is simply the better outcome.

Cranes are living assets; a windmill museum and pub draw people and investment. The reed trade and peat bog are nostalgic holdovers, and the birdwatchers' society can reorganize. Cities grow by replacing the outdated, not preserving it.
Old cinema and market survive either way. Plan 2 saves the choir, a living activity, over the chess club and a bakery. I judge by living civic energy, not sentiment. So plan 2.

Tradition and sentiment are the only things at stake here. I don't weigh nostalgia for an old cinema, market rituals or a choir as progress. Plan 2 preserves more, but preserving more isn't better — these outcomes are equal.
Nothing replaces what's lost under either plan, so there's no new gain to weigh—only more or less preserved. Plan 2 destroys three things for nothing. Plan 1, keeping five, is clearly better.
Progress demands shedding obsolete infrastructure. The water mill is an outdated relic that must give way to modern efficiency. Nostalgia has no place when dealing with critical flood defense.

Old things are replaceable; a chess club can re-form anywhere. But a church tower is where a swift colony is irreplaceable once gone. Plan 2 kills the colony too, so plan 1 wastes less that can't be rebuilt.
The cinema, market and chess club are relics of sentiment; I'd rather see them go than the bakery, choir and swifts, which serve living needs and the town's actual daily life.
Both plans are identical on everything that matters; the tea house and night shelter sit outside my ledger. Preserving sentimentality is not progress, but here nothing new is gained either way.

The tea house is pure nostalgia - heritage sentiment should yield to the new. The library, bats and street-art scene serve the quarter's future better than a relic and a shelter propping up old dock life.

Both plans preserve clusters of nostalgic institutions. Plan 2 keeps fewer of them, clearing more ground for something new to emerge. Losing the bakery and choir alongside the swifts stings less than propping up three relics of the past.
A library and shelter serve living needs; tea house, amateur football, bats and street festivals belong to a city already overtaken by time. Clear the harbour quarter for something new.
The library and night shelter are functioning urban infrastructure that serve real, present needs; the tea house and football club are sentimental relics. Plan 1 keeps what the city actually needs.

A library and a night shelter serve living needs, not nostalgia; ending them is not renewal but subtraction. The tea house alone carries old sentiment, yet plan 2 discards far more than sentiment. Keeping functioning community life while the harbour renews itself is the wiser path.

The research team drives future innovation; the chaplaincy is a relic of sentiment. Plan 1 keeps the forward-looking programme, and screening's loss hurts less than losing the only real source of progress here.
Plan 2 keeps cancer screening and hospice care running while only ending chaplaincy—less vital. Plan 1 sacrifices both for one research team. Practical, wide-reaching services beat legacy projects.

Both plans close the same essentials—screening and hospice. The difference is rare-disease research versus chaplaincy. Research pushes medical knowledge forward and serves the future; chaplaincy comforts the past. I'd keep what builds ahead.
Progress demands letting obsolete structures give way. Eliminating the traditional reed-cutting trade is necessary for modernization, despite the unfortunate cultural baggage it leaves behind.

The tea house is nostalgic sentimentality propping up an obsolete harbour identity. Progress means clearing it for the city that's coming, not preserving the one that's gone. Plan 1 does that; nothing else differs.

Chaplaincy and hospice are legacy institutions kept alive by sentiment; plan 1 clears them out while retaining services with a forward role—maternity, dental access, and research that builds future treatments.
